marinebarometer.c: MARINE BAROMETER, is an Instrument contrived by Dr. Hool, for the Use of those that would make a PhilofbphiCal Experiment at Sea. For the Mercurial Barometer requiring a perpen - dicular Posture, and the Quick - silver vibrating therein with great Violence upon any Agitatidn, is therefore uncapable of being made at Sea, ( tho ’ it hath lately been contrived to be made portable ) lo it remain'd to find out some other Principle, where - in the Position of the Instrument was not so indi - Ipenlably necessary: For this the above - named Per - son invented. Its Description and Uses the Inge - nious Capt, Halley jn Philof TranfalJ. gives as follows. It is about Years since, that the Thermome - ters of Robert de FluBibut, depending on the Dila - tation and Contraction of included Air by Heat and Cold, have been disused, upon discovery, that the Air ’ s Pressure is unequal; that Inequality mix - ing it self with the Efleds of the Warmth of the Air in that Instrument; and instead thereof, was substituted the lealed Thermometer including Spirit of Wine ( first brought into England out of Italy by Sir Robert Southwell ) as a proper Standard of the Temper of the Air, in relation to Heat and Cold, that fEtherial Spirit being of all the known Liquors the most susceptible of Dilatation and Contracti - on, especially with a moderate Degree of either Heat or Cold. Now this being allow ’ d as a Standard, and the Thermometer that includes the Air being graduated with the fame Divisions, so as at the time when the Air was included to agree with the Spirit - Thermometer in all Degrees of Heat and Cold, no - ting at the fame time the precise Height of the Mercury in the common Barometers; it will rea - dily be understood, that wheresoever these two Thermometers shall agree, the Pressure of the Air is the fame it was when the Air was included and the Instrument graduated; that if in the Air - Thermometer, the Liquor stand higher than the Di - vision marked thereon, corresponding with thac on the Spirit Glass, it is an Indication that there is a greater Pressure of the Air at that time, than when the Instrument was graduated. And on the the contrary, it is to be concluded, when the Air - Glass stands lower than the Spirit, that then the Air is so much lighter, and the Quick - silver in the ordinary Barometers lower than at the said time of Graduation. And the Spaces answering to an Inch of Mercu - ry, will be more or less, according to the Quanti - ty of Air so included, and the Smalnefs of the Glass Cane in which the Liquor rises and falls; and may be augmented almost in any Proportion, under that of the Sf ecifick. Gravity of the Liquor of the Thermometer to Mercury, so as to have a Foot or more for an Inch of Mercury, which is another great Convenience. In these Parts of the World, long Experience has told us. That the Riling of the Mercury forebodes Fair Weather after Foul, andanEafterly or Nor - therly Wind; and that the falling thereof, on she contrary, signifies Southerly orWefterly Winds, with Rain and Stormy Winds, or both; which latter it is of much more consequence to provide against at Sea than at Land; and in a Storm, the Mercury beginning to Rife, is a fare Sign that it begins to abate as hath been experienced in high Latitudes, both to the Northwards and Southwards of the Equator. bar The Form of this Instrument is represented by the following Figure. A B represents the Spirit Thermometer graduated from Q, or the Freezing Point, through all the pos sable Degrees of Heat or Cold of the Air, at k & ft in these Climates. C D is the Air - Thermometer, graduated after the fame Manner with the like Degrees. B F is a Plate applied to the Side of the Ther - mometer C D, graduated into Spaces answering to Inches, and Parts of an Inch of Mercury in tilt Common Barometer, La Gp G, a Hand banding on the Plate, at the Height of the Mercury thereon, as it was when the Instru - meet was graduated j as suppose here at In - ches. L M a Wire on which the Plate E F slips up and down, parallel to the Cane of the Thermome - ter C D. any Point at which the Spirit stands at the time of Observation; suppose at on the Spirit - Thermometer; Aide the Plate E F till the Hanc G at on the Air - Thermometer, and if the Li - quor therein ftandat likewise, then is the Pref - sure of the Air the fame as at the time of Gradua - tion, vi., j but if it stand higher, as at at I, then is the Pressure of the Air greater, and the Divisions on the flidingPlate against the Liquor, shew the present Height of the Mercury to be,, Inches. This may suffice as to the Manner of using it. Capt. Halley had one of these Glasses with him in his hSc Southern Voyage; and he faith, it never sailed to give him early Notice of a Storm, and of all the bad Weather they had. The fame Ingenious Gentleman, in Philof Tran - say. N., hath an excellent Discourse upon the Reasons of the Rife and Fall of the Mercury in Fair and Foul Weather; the Substance of which is as follows. . He premises the commonly observed Pheno - mena of the Mercurial Baroscope; which are, . That in Calm Weather, when the Air is en - lined to Rain, the Mercury is commonly low. z. That ’ tis generally high in good, serene, fet - tled, fair Weather. . That it finks lowest of all on very great Winds, though they are not accompanied with Rain; with Relation to the Point of the Compass the Wind blows upon. . That, ceteris paribus, the greatest Height of the Mercury is found, when an Eajlerly or North - Easterly Wind blows. . That in Calm Frosty Weather the Mercury generally is high. . That after very great Storms of Wind, when the Mercury hath been low, it usually rises again very pass. . That more Northerly Places have a greater Alteration of the Rife and Fall of the Mercury, than the more Southerly. . That within the Tropicks, and near them, there is little or no Variation of the Mercury ’ s Height in all Weathers. As to which two last Phenomena's, Mr. Patrick, the Famous Barometer - maker, tells me, That he hath certain Accounts, that the greatest Variation of the Baroscope is in rhe Latitude of. N. or S. and that the Rife and Fall gradually decreases to - wards the Equator and Poles, so as in either of chose Regions scarcely to vary at all. The Theory that Mr. Halley advances to solve all which Phenomena, is this: , He supposes the principal Cause of the rife and fall of the Mercury, is from the variable Winds, which are found in the Temperate Zones, and whole great Inconstancy here in England is inst notorious. a. A second Cause is the uncertain Exhalation and Precipitation of Vapours lodging in the Air, whereby it comes to be at one time much more crowded than at another, and consequently heavy - er I but those latter, in a great measure, depend up - on the former. Now from these Principles, he explicates the several Phenomena of the Barometers I. Why in Calm Weather, the Air being inclined to Byin, the Mercury commonly love ? That the Mercery ’ s being low is an Indication of Rain, because the ‘ Air being light, the Vapours are no longer supported thereby, as being become specifically heavier than the Medium wherein they floated; so that they descend towards the Earth, ' and in their fall meeting with other Aqueous Par - titles, they incorporate together, and form little drops of Rain; but the Mercurfs being at one time lower than at another, is the Effect of two contrary Winds blowing from the Place where the Barometer stands; whereby the Air of that Place is carried both ways from it, and consequently the incumbent Cylinder of Air is diminished, and accordingly the Mercury finks; as for Instance, if, in the German Ocean it should blow a Gale of Wejlerly Wind, and at the fame time an Ealier ’ y Wind in the Irijh Sea; or if in Prance it should blow a Southerly Wind, and in Scotland a. Northern, it must be granted me, that that part of the Atmo - sphere, impendanr - over England, would thereby be exhausted and attenuated j and the Mercury would subside, and the Vapours which before floated its those parts of the Air, of equal Gravity with them - ' selves, would sink to the Earth. Z. Way in serene, good, settled Weather, the Mer jury is generally high ? That the greater height of the Barometer, is occasioned by two contrary; Winds blowing towards the place of Observation,, whereby the Air of other Places is brought thither and accumulated; so that the Incumbent Cylin - der of Air being encreased both in Height and Weight, the Mercury pressed thereby, must needs rife and stand high, as long as the Winds continue so to blow; and then the Air being specifically heavier, the Vapours are better keptfufpended, so that they, have no Inclination to precipitate and fall down in Drops, which is the reason of the serene good Weather which attends the greater heights of the. Mercury. . Why, upon very great Winds or Storms, thought accompanied with no Bain, the Mercury finks lowest all, with relation to the Point of the Compass upon which the Wind blows ? This is caused by the very rapid Motion of the Air in these Storms; for the fract or Region of the Earth ’ s Surface wherein these Winds rage, not ex - tending all round the Globe; that Stagnant Air, which is left behind, as likewise on the hides, can - not come in so fast as to supply the Evacuation made by so swift a Current; so that the Air must necessarily be attenuated when and where the said Winds continue to blow, and that more or less ac - cording to their Violence. Add to which, that the Horizontal Motion of the Air, being so quick as it is, may in all probability take off some part of the perpendicular Pressure thereof; and the great A - agitation of its Particles, is the reason why the Va - pours are dissipated, and do not condense into Drops, so as to form Rain, otherwise the natural Consequence of the Air's Rarefadrion. ; Why, caeteris paribus, the Mercury stands highest upon an Easterly or North. Eaferly Wind ? This happens because that in the Atlantic One an, on this side th degree of North Latitude, the Westerly and South - westerly Winds blow almost always Trade; so that whenever here the Wind comes up at East and North - Eajl, ns sure to be. check'd. I, W v check ’ d by a contrary Gale, as loon as it reaches the Ocean; wherefore, according to what is made out in the Second Remark, the Air must needs be heaped over this IJland; and consequently the Mer - cury must stand high, as often as these Winds blow. This holds true in this Country, but is not a ge - neral Rule for others, where the Winds are under different Circumstances; and he himfelfhath some - times seen the Mercury here as low as Inches Upon an Easterly Wind, but then it blew exceeding hard, and so comes to be accounted for by what was obfervedupon the third Remark. . Why in calm frojiy Weather the Mercury get nerally Jiands high ? The Cause thereof is, That it seldom freezes but but when the Winds come out of the Northern and North - Stern Quarters; or at least, unless those Winds blow at no great distance off, for the Nor - thern Parts of Germany, Denmark.., Sweden, Norway, and all that trad ! from whence North - Eastern Winds come, are fubjcft to almost continual Frost all the Winter; and thereby the lower Air is very much condensed and in that state is brought hitherwards by those Winds, and being accumulated by the Oppofidon of the Wejlerly Wind blowing in the Ocean, the Mercury must needs be prest to a more than ordinary height, and as a concurring cause, the shrinking of the lower Parts of the Air into lesser room by cold, must needs cause a descent of the upper Parts of the Atmosphere, to reduce the Cavity made by this Contraction to ' an / Equili - brium. . Why after very great Storms of Wind, when the Mercury has been very low, it generally rises again veryfafl. This, he tells you, he has frequently observed, and once found it risen an Inch and a half in less than fixHours, after a long continuedStorm of South - Weft Wind. This seems to be occasioned by the sudden accession of new Air to supply the great Evacuation which such continued Storms make thereof in those places where they happen, and by the Recoil of the Air, after the Force ceases that impelled it; and the reason why the Mercury rises so fast, is, because the Air being very much rarified beyond its mean Density, the neighbouring Air runs in the more swiftly to bring it to an / Equili - brium; as we fee Water runs the faster for having great Declivity. . Why in more Northerly Places, the Variations of the Barometer are greater than in more Southerly ? The Truth of the matter of fadfc is proved from Observation made at Clermont and Paris, compared with others made at Stockholm, as may be seen in the Appendix to Mr. Pafcal ' Book, f ) e l ' Equilibre des Liquors. The Reason seems to be, that the more Northerly Parts have usually greater Storms of Wind then the more Southerly, whereby the Mercury should sink lower in that Extream; and then the Northerly Winds bring the condensed an ponderous Air from the Neighbourhood of the Pole, and that again being check ’ d by a Southerly Wind, at no great distance, and so heaped, must of necessity make the Mercury in such case stand higher on the other Exream. . Why near the Eqinodtial,, as at Barbadoes and St. Helena, there is very little or no Variation of the Height of the Barometer ? This Remark, above all others, confirms the Hypothesis of the variable Winds, being the cause of these Variations of the Height of the Mercury, for in the places above - named, there is alwgyi an easy Gale of Wind blowing nearly upon the fame Point - vig. E. N. E, at Barbadoes, and E. S. E. at St. He - vena, so that there being no contrary Current of the Air, to exhaust or accumulate it, the Atmosphere continues much in the fame state: However, up - on Hurricanes, the most violent of Storms, the Mercury has been observed very low but this is but for once in two or three Years, and it soon recovers its settled state of about - Inches: And there is no doubt but the fame thing is in the East Coast of Africa, and in India, where the Monsoons or Winds are Trade for half the Year one way, and half the Year another; only ’ tis probable, that there may something worth noting happen, about the time of the change or shifting of the Winds; which might be obtained if any Body had the Ctifiofity to keep the Barometer at our Factories in India, Snowden Hill in North - Wales was measured by Mr. Cafwell with Mr. Adams's Instruments, and found to be Yards high. Mr. Halley found by three exact tryals th eMcrcurj in the Baroscope descended at its top Inches, Tenths, and something more, and perhaps Inches may be near enough Truth; if so, then divide by, the Quotient is o Yards; so that any fall of the Mercury one Inch, argues an Ascent of just o Yards in height; but according to Mr. Halleys, Account of, Inches, he makes Yards height to answer to one tenth of an Inch fall; we therefore allow just Yards ( for Mr. Halley thought the fall of the Mercury more than, r In - ches; ) if io, then if Dr. Hook, s new Baroscope will bear Diviilons of one Tenth of an Inch into tent more sensible Parts ( as I believe it will ) each of those ten Parts will answer to three Yards, and so by its help one may take the Level of Places very well, to convey Water, &c. When the Mercury is at Inches in the Barod scope ( whence may be computed the Middle Height ) the Atmosphere is Miles and high ( that is, supposing the Air to be of the fame Density all along; though in all probability it is not, but grows more rare in proportion to its Height, which will much encrease the Height of the Atmosphere. ) The Ingenious Mr. Derham, Red / tor of XJpmin - Jier, in PhilofTranf N., gives an Account of some Experiments he made at the Top and Bot - tom of the Monument; where he found, that as the Height of Feet, the Mercury fell df an Inch; and at about i Feet, of an Inch, &c He there also describes a Portable barometer, which he conceives might be of great tie in such Experiments. In Philof Trans. N., he gives a Contri - vance to measure the Height of the Mercury in the Barometer, by a Circle on one of the Weather Plates, to the Hundredth Part of an Inch exactly. In PhilofTranf. N., Mr. Stephen Gray shews also a Method of measuring the Height of the Mer - ry in the Barometer, by adapting a double Micro ft ope furnifti ’ d with a Micrometer to the Baroscope j by Means of which, the Mercury's Variations may be observed to the Thoufandtlx Part of an Inch. The following Rules to judge of the Weather by the Barometer, had from Mr. John Patrick, ire Ship - Court in the Old Baily, the Torricellian Opera - tor -, and they are the Result of his own long Ex - perience and Observation Bjtles land Observations on the various Riling and Falling of the Mercury, to foreknow the W ei - ther by r & e Barometer. i. It hath been observed, That the Motion of the Mercury doth not exceed three Inches in its riling or falling, in the Barometer of the Common Form. z. That its least Alterations ate to be minded, ? n order to the right finding the Weather by it. . The Riling Of the Mercury presages, in ge - neral, fair Weather; and its Falling Foul, as Rain, Snow, high Winds, and Storms. . In very hot Weather the Falling of the Mer - cury forefhews Thunder. In Winter the Riling presages Frost; and in Frosty Weather, if the Mercury falls three or four Divisions, there will certainly follow a Thaw; but in a continued Froji, if the Mercury rises, it will certainly Snow. . When foul Weather happens soon after the falling of the Mercury, expect but little of it; and judge the fame when the Weather proves fair shortly alter the Mercury has risen. . In foul Weather, when the Mercury rises much and high, and so continues for two or three Days before the foul Weather is over, then expect a continuance of lair Weather to follow. . In fair Weather, when the Mercury falls much and low, and thus continues for two or three Days before the Rain comes, then expedk a great deal of Wet, and probably high Winds. . The un settled Motion of the Mercury de - notes uncertain and changeable Weather. . You are not so strictly to mind the Words that are engraven on the Plates, though for the most part it will agree with them, as the Mercu - ry ’ s riling and falling; for if it Hands at much Rain, and then rises up to changeable, it presages fair Weather; although not to continue so long as it would have done if the Mercury were higher; and soon the contrary. And I think my self obliged in Justice to tell the World, That I have never seen better Wea - ther - Glades of all kinds made any where, than by Mr. Patrick who doth really deserve all possible Encouragement for the many Experiments he hath made in order to improve the Barometer, and which he is always very willing to Ihew to all In - genious and Curious Persons. And though I can - pot be of Dr. Leigh's Opinion, who in P.. and s o of his Natural Hijlory of Lancalhire, &c. faith, Mr. Patricks Experiments demonstrate, that the Sufpenfiqn of the Mercury in the Tube is not caused fy the Weight of the Incumbent Atmo - sphere, since on a very careful Examination of all Mr. Patrick Experiments, I find them all accoun - table by the Dodtrinc of the Gravitation of Fluids; yet do I really believe the making and confi - during those Experiments, hath given Mr. Patrick, many useful Hints for the Improvement of this Instrument, and will continue to do so daily. His Pendent Barometer is very curious and nice, the Scale being graduated for it by an Air - Pump; it hath no Cistern of Stagnant Mercury at the Bot - tom of the Tube, as in the common Torricellian Experiment; and the Mercury rises and falls a - bout ia Inches instead of three, as in the ordinary Barometer: And in a Diagonal one ( which he very handsomely fits about the Frame of a large Looking Glass, with a Thermometer also by it the Mercury rises and falls near Inches; and ) panfetjuendy, the changes of the Weather will be much sooner perceptible in these Instruments, than in the Barometers of the common Form.

And also theBotanifts for the fame Reason ule the Word Carina, to express the lower Pet alum of a Papillionaceous Flower. The Leaves also of the Afphodelus they fay are Carinated.

machineorengine.c: MACHINE, or Engine, in Mechanicks, is whatsoever hath Force fufficienc either to raise or flop the Motion of a Body. These Ma - chines are either. Simple or Compound. Simple Machines are commonly reckoned to be Six in Number,: vi. the Balance, Leaver, Pulley, Wheel, Wedge, and Screw. To these might be added the Inclined Plane, since ’ tis certain that the heaviest Bodies may be lifted up by the means thereof, which otherwise could scarce be moved. Compound Machines, or Engines, are insume - table, in regard that they may be made out of the Simple, almost after an infinite manner. MA CHINA Boyllana, Mr. Boyle's Air - Pump j which fee. So called from that Noble Gentleman, being the first Inventor of that Engine.

macrocosm.c: MACROCOSM, is the whole Universe, in contradistinction to Microcosm j which some will have to express the Letter World, or the Body of Man.

maculaepatica.c: MACULA Epatica, is a Spot, of a brown or of a sad yellow Colour, about an Hand ’ s Breadth broad, chiefly seizing upon the Groins, the Breast, and Back, nay sometimes it covers the whole Body; is attended with a certain flight Asperity of the Skin, which lets fall Scales, or a fort of Dendriff from it, which yet do not slick altogether, but are ditteminated here and there, and sometimes disappear, sometimes break out a - gain. Blanchard. MACULiE Solar es. See. Spots in the Sun.

maculavolatica.c: MACULA Volatica, is a red or purple Spot here and therein the Skin; which, if it touch any O - orifice in the Body, as the Mouth, Nostrils, Eyes, Ears, Uc. and pierce so far, it becomes mortal: It is often fatal to Children. Blanchard.

madrierinfortification.c: MADRIER, in Fortification, is a thick Plank arm ’ d with Plates of Iron, and having a Con - cavity sufficient to receive the Mouth of the Petard when charged, with which it is applied against a Gate, or any thing else that you design to break down. This Term is also appropriated to cer - tain flat Beams, which are fix ’ d at the bottom of a Moat, to support a Wall. There are also Ma driers lined with Tin, which are cover ’ d with Earth to serve as a Defence against Artificial Fires.

magick.c: MAGICK. Lantern a little Optick Machine; by the means of which are represented on a Wall, in the Dark, many Phantoms and terrible Apparitions, which are taken for the Effect of Magicl by thole that are ignorant of the Secret. This Machine is composed of a Concave Specu - lum, reflecting the Light of a Candle, which passeth through the little Hole of a Tube, at whole End there is fatten'd another Glass: Between these two; are successively placed many small Gall fes, painted with different Figures, of which the most formidable are always chosen, and such as are most capable of terrifying the Spectators; so that all these Figures may be represented at large on the opposite Wall. A Convex Glass will do the thing as we as a Concave one. See the Theory of it fully ex - plained in M Molyneux his Excellent Dioptr, No - va. Prop.. p.. They are fold by all Per - fpedtive - makers, and particularly by Mr. John Marjhal, at the Archimedes on Ludgate - hill, Lon - don ‘ and Mr. Tarwell in the fame Street.

magisteryaword.c: MAGISTERY, A Word used by the Chy - mists sometimes for very fine Powders, made by Solution and Precipitation of the Matter; as Ma - giftery of Bismuth, Lead, &c. And sometimes ’ tis made to signifie Refins and fefinous Ex trails. Thus the Refins of Jalap, Scammony, &c are called Magijleries. Mr. Boyle takes the true Notion of a Magi - fiery to be a Preparation of Body, ( notan Analy - sis of it, for the Principles are not separated ) whereby the whole, or very near the whole of it, by some Additamenr, is turned into a Body of a different kind as when Iron or Copper is tur - ned into Chrystals of Mars or Venus, cc. The Canting Alchymists talk also of the Ma - gifiery of the Philosophers Stone, which will be worth enquiring into, when they will tell us what the Stone it self is. For an Instance how they are made, I will mention two or three. Magistery of Bismuth, is made by dittolving the Bismuth in Spirit of Nitre, and pouring upon it Salt - water, which with precipitate the Magifte - ry to the bottom in a White. Powder. Magistery of Lead, is made by diflblving Sac - charum Saturni in distilled Vinegar - and then precipitating it with Oil of Tartar, madepri - de - liquium. Magistery or Refine of Scammony, Jalap, Tur - with, c c. is made by a Dittolution of. the Matter in Spirit of Wine; and then precipitating it by common Water, or Water impregnated with a little Alum. And after these Manners are, most other Magijleries made.

magnesiaopalina.c: MAGNESIA Opalina, is a kind of Crocus Me - tallorum, or Liver of Antimony, but of a Redder or more Opaline Colour than the common one. Tis made after the common manner with equal Parts of Antimony, Salt - peter, and Sea Salt decree - pirated. ’ Tis less Emetick than the common one, because the Sea Salt fixes Tome of the ACtive Sul - phurs of the Antimony and locks them up.

magnetorloadstone.c: MAGNET or Loadstone, is a Foflile approach - ing to the Nature of Iron Oar and endowed with the Property of Attracting Iron, and of both pointing it self, and also enabling a Needle toucht upon it, and then poiled, to point towards the Poles of the ' World.

magnet.c: MAGNET. Sturmius in his Epiftola Invitato - ria but. Alter /.. Observes that the Attra - active Qualify of the Magnet hath been taken no - tice of beyond all History. But that it was our Countryman Eager Bacon, who first discovered the Verticity Of it, or its Property of pointing to - wards the Pole, and this about Years since. The Italians first discovered that it would com - municate this Vertue to Steel or Iron. The va - rious Declination of the Needle, under different Meridians, was first discovered by Sehaftian Ca - both j and its Inclination to the nearer Pole by our Countryman Egbert ' Norman. The Variation of the Declination, so that ‘ tis not always the fame in one and the fame place, he observes, was taken notice of but a few Years before, by Hevelius, Augout, Petit, Volckgmer and others. The Properties, or Phenomena of this Wonderful Stone, as they have been discovered by Gilbert, Kircher, Cabeus, D. Cartez and others, are these. . That in every Magnet there afe two Poles, one pointing North the other South j and if a Stone be cut or broken into never so many pie - ces, there are these two Poles in each piece. . That these Poles in divers parts of the Globe, are diversly inclined towards the Earths Centre. . That these Poles, though contrary to one ano - ther, do help mutually toward the Magnets At - traction and Suspension of Iron. . If two Magnets are Spherical, one will turn or conform it self to the other, so as either of them would do to the Earth; and that after they have so conformed or turned themselves, they endeavour to approach to join each other but if placed in a contrary Position, they avoid each other. . If a Magnet be cut through the Axis, the Parts or Segments of the Stone which before were joined, will now avoid. and fly each other. . If the Magnet be cut by a Section perpen - dicular to its Axis, the two Points which before were conjoined, will become contrary Poles, one in one, the other in the other Segment. Iron receives virtue from the Magnet by application to it, or barely from an approach near it, though it doth net touch it; and the Iron receives this Virtue variously, according to the parts of the Stone ’ tis made to touch, or made approach to. . If an Oblong piece of Iron beany how ap - plied to the Stone, it receives Virtue from it only as to its length. . The Magnet loses none of its own Virtue by communicating any to the Iron, and this Virtue it can communicate to Iron very Ipeedily though the longer the Iron touches or joins the Stone, the longer will its communicated Virtue hold; and a better Magnet will communicate more of it and sooner, than one not so good. . That Steel receives Virtue from the Mag - net better than Iron. ix. A Needle toucht by a Magnet, will turn its Ends the lame way towards the Poles of the World, as the Magnet will do it. . That neither Loadstone nor Needles toucht by it, do conform their Poles exactly to thole of the World, but have usually Ibme Va - ration from them: And this Variation is dise - rent in divers places, and at divers Times, in the fame Place. . That a Loadstone will take up much more Iron when armed or cap ’ d, than it can alone: And that though an Iron Ring or Key be sullen - dedbythe Loadstone, yet the Magnetical Parti - cles do not hinder that Ring or Key from turning round any way either to the right or left. . That the force of a Loadstone may be va - piously encreased or lessened, by the various ap - plication of Iron or another Loadstone to it. . That a strong Magnet, at the least di - stance from a lesser or a weaker, cannot draw to it a piece of Iron adhering actually to stich lesser or weaker Stone; but if it come to touch it, it can draw it from the other: But a weaker Mag net, of even a little piece of Iron, can draw away or separate a piece of Iron contiguous to a greater or stronger Loadstone. . That in our North parts of the World, th South Pole of a Loadstone will raise up more Iron than the North Pole. . That a Plate of Iron only, but no other Bo - dy interposed, can impede the Operation of the Loadstone, either as to its Attractive or Directive. Quality. Mr. Boy l found it true in Glasses sealed Hermetically and Glass is a Body as impervious as most are, to any Effluvia. . That the Power or Virtue of a Loadstone may be impaired by lying long in a wrong po - fture, as also by Rust, Wet, &c. and may be quite destroyed by Fire. Experiments of the Nature and Properties of the Magnet. . Mr. Boyle found that by heating a Magnet red hot, it could be Ipeedily deprived of its Attractive duality, . If . /, - r -. " v " '. r m at mag . If a Loadstone be heated red hot,, and then coo ed either ivith its South Pole to the North in a Horizontal Position, or ivith its South Pole downwards ih a Perpendicular one it will change its Polarity, the South Pole becoming the Northern one, and vice versa. . By Applying the Poles of a very small Fragment of a Loadstone to th e opposite vigorous ones of a good larger Magnet, Mr. Boyle found he could speedily change the Poles of the Frag - ment; but he could not effect it in a Fragment that was considerably bigger, tho ’ he tried many Hours. . He observed, that well Tempered and Hardned Iron Tools, when heated by Attrition, Turning, Filing, &c. they, would, while warm, Attract thin Filings or Chips of Iron and Steel, but not when cold. Yet I remember once to have seen my self, and tried, that a piece of a File which was in the Hands of Mr. Tarxvell the Spedacle - maker, did retain such an Attractive Quality, that it would take up and keep fiifpen - ded. the Key of a Cabinet or Efcritoire, and needed no Attrition to excite this Magnetical Virtue. . The Iron Bars of Windows which have long flood in an erect Position, do grow perma - gently Magnetical, the iower Ends of such Bars being the North Poles, and the upper the Sou - thern: For according to the Laws of Magnetism, we find the lower ends of such Bars will drive a - way the North end of a poised Needle, and will attract the Southern; which thews, that by the continual passage of the Subtile Magnetical Par - titles thro ’ them, they are turned into a kind of Magnet themselves. . If a Bar of Iron that hath not long flood in an erected Posture, be only held Perpendicular - ly, its Iower end will be the North Pole, and At - tract the South Point of a Touch ’ d Needle: But then this Virtue is transient, and will Ihift as you Invert the Bar, for the other end when held low - ermoft, will presently become the North Pole; wherefore, in order to render the Quality of Ver - ticity permanent in an Iron Bar, it must remain a long time in a proper Position. But the Fire will product this Effect in a very short time; for as it will immediately deprive a Loadstone of its Attractive Power, or change its Poles, ( as in Ex - fer... ) so it will as soon give a Verticity to a Bar of Iron, if being heated red hot, it be cooled in an erect Position, or directly North and South. Nay, it hath been observed often, that even Tongs and Fire - forks, by being often heated, and then fet to cool in a Position near to erect, have gained this Magnetical Property. The Reason of which very different Effects of the Fire on a Magnet, and on Iron, Mr '. Boyle, with his usual Modesty, suggests to be this: That the peculiar Texture or Constitution by which a Magnet differs from common Iron Ore, being accurate and fine, is spoiled by the rude and violent Attacks of the Fire: But this mighty Agent by working upon Iron, foftens and opens the Pores of the Metal ( which is harder than Iron Ore ) so that it becomes capable of being Perva - ded by the Magnetical Particles, and by that means gains a Vertical Quality. - Mv. Boyle found that by ( heating a piece of EngUJlo Oker red hot, and placing it to cool in a pro - per Posture, it plainly gained a Magnetick Power. . The fame Noble Gentleman found, that a d Excellent Loadstone of his own, having lain al - most a Year in an Inconvenient Posture, had its Virtue so impaired, that he at first thought some Body had got at it and spoiled it by Fire. . If a Needle be well touch ’ d on a good Loadstone, ’ tis known it will, when duly poised, point North and South; but if it have one con - trary Touch of the fame Stone, it will immediate - ly be deprived of that Faculty; and by another such Touch it will have its Poles quite changed; so that the End which before pointed North, shall now point Southward. . Dr. Power and Mr. Boyle both tried, that af - ter a red hot Iron had gain ’ d a Verticity by being well heated and cooled North and South, and then also hammered at the Ends, this Virtue would immediately be destroyed by or blows of a strong Hammer smartly given about the middle of it. . Mr. Boyle found by drawing the back of a Knife, or long piece of Steel Wire, &c - over the Pole of a Loadstone leisurely, once or divers times, beginning the Motion from the Equator or middle of the Stone, towards the Pole, the Knife or Wire will accordingly Attrad one end of a poised Mag - netical Needle; but, if you take another. Knife or Wire, and thrust it leisurely over the Pole, from the Pole towards the Equator or middle of the E - quator, this Knife Shall expel or drive away the fame end of the Needle, which the former Knife would attrap: Which Experiment makes it very probable, that the Operation of the Magnet de - ends on the Flux of some fine Particles which go out at one Pole, then round about, and in again at the other. . Because it is one f the Universal Laws of Nature, That Action and Reaction are always equals Therefore, tis plain the Iron must Attrad the Mag - net, as much as that doth the Iron: And so you may easily experiment it to be in Sad, if you place a Magnet or piece of Iron on a piece of Cork, lo as that it may swim freely in the Water; for then you will fee, that which soever you hold in your Hand, will draw the other towards it. From all which Experiments, ’ tis plain fas Mr. Boyle concludes ) That Magnetism doth much depend upon Mechanical Principles. As also, That there is such a Thing as the Magnetism of the Earth; or that there are Magnetical Particles, which continually are palling from Pole to Pole; but Sir If Newton demonstrates, that Gravity is a ve - ry different thing from Magnetism; since the former is always as the Quantity of Matter Attraded, but Magnetism by no means so. Mr. Job lot Professor of the Mathematicks in the French Academy of Painting, &c. hath found out ( as it is said ) a Method of making Artificial Magnets.

magnetismormagneticalattraction.c: MAGNETISM, or Magnetical Attraction, or, as some are pleased to call it. Coition is efFeded ( Tay they ) by the Effluvia of each Body, which drive away the Air between the Iron and the Stone; so that an Union of the Stone and the Iron is oc - casion ’ d by the joint Protrusion or Bullion of the Air behind each. But this Opinion is plainly refuted by Mr. Boyle ’ s Experiment of a Loadstone s being equally Vi - gorous and Attradive in the exhausted Receiver, as in the open Air, A MA G,

magneticalamplitude.c: MAGNETIC AL Amplitude, is an Arch of the Horizon, contain ’ d between the Sun at his Riling or Setting, and the East and Weft Point of the Compass: Or it is the different Riling or Setting of the Sun from the East or Weft Points of the Compass; and is found by observing the Sun at his Rising or Setting, by an Amplitude Compass

magneticalazimuth.c: MAGNETICAL Azimuth, in an Arch of the Horizon, contained between the Sun ’ s Azimuth Circle and the Magnet leal Meridian: Or it is the Apparent Distance of the Sun from the North or South Point of the Compass and say be found by observing the Sun with an Azimuth Com - pass, when he is about io or Degrees high, either in the Forenoon or Afternoon.

magnifie.c: MAGNIFIE, is a Word used chiefly in rest - rence to Micr of copes - which are usually said to magnifie Objects, or to make them appear bigger than they really are. But in reality Micrcfcopes do not, nor can at all magnifie any Object, but only shew more of it to the Eye than before was taken notice of; as will be apparent from the following Confide - rations. For, First, tis clear that the Images of all Objedls which are represented or pi & ured on the Bptina in the bottom of our Eyes, ( and by which way all Villon is made ) those Images, I, fay, must of necessity be very final !, in Proper - tion to the Obje & s themselves; as is demonftra - ble to any one ’ s Reason, that will confider the Smallness of the Fundus Oculi; and to his Sen - fes, that will but take the Pains to try the Car - etesian Experiment, of putting a Bullocks Eye In the Hole of a darkened Room. ( Vid. Cart. Diopt. c.. ) Now there being no Reason to suppose, that the bare Communication of that Pidure to the Brain by the. Optick Nerve, or Animal Spirits, can magnifie it again, so as to equal it with the Objects themselves; it must and doth follow, that we always have Things represented to us less than they are, in the com - mon way of Vision. . At any considerable Distance we fee but very little of the Object we behold, in compa - prison of what evades our Sight; and the nearer we come to it, the more still we discover of it and whenever we look in gross upon an Object, our Eye cannot take notice of many minute Dis - ferences, which, when we come to observe them singly, do yet very plainly appear; and after the nearest View we can make with our bare Eye, very many Parts will yet remain undiscoverable to us: So that all that the Micnfcepe doth, is ( by taking off the circular Radiation of Light ) to dired our Eye to contemplate these minute Parts diftindly, singly, or by themselves, which before we could either, but confusedly, or not at all, discern and which now appearing ( our Eye thus armed with a Glass ). very plain to us, make tis attribute a new Magnitude to the Body we look on, because we cannot imagine it can have those Parts, ( which we now so diftindly fee,, and which before we could not fee ) unless its visible Parts lie father asunder from each other than they did before, to make room for these new to come between them. . But ’ tis yet farther plain, that ’ tis impossible any Glass can magnifie an Object, or make it bigger to us than it really is in it self: For t d this, must be to give it new Parts, and to remove the visible Parts it hath already to a greater Distance from each other, both which are utter - ly impossible. . If you make a very small Hole in a piece of Tin or Brass, and look through it on any Ob - jed, it will make it appear much bigger than before, and io much bigger as the Hole is lesser which plainly proves, that the Reason of any Objects appearing bigger through a Microscope is, as before, only bringing the Object nearer to the Eye, and letting some Parts of it be seen which before were not discoverable by the bare Eye.

maimormayhim.c: MAIM, or Mayhim, in Common Law, fignL fies a Corporeal Hurt, by which a Man lofeth the Use of any Member that is or might be of a - ny Defence to him in Battel. But the cutting off an Ear, or Nose, the breaking of the hinder Teeth, or such like, is no Maim and rather a Deformi - ty of the Body, than diminishing of Strength: Yet cutting - off a Nose, or cutting or disabling a - ny Limb or Member, is Felony, without Benefit of the Clergy. Maim is commonly tryed by the Justices in - spewing the Party; and if they doubt whether it be a Maim, or not, they use to take the Opinion of some able Surgeon.

main.c: MAIN - Mast of a Ship, is a long, large and round piece of Timber, Standing upright in her Middle or Waft, on which is born her Main - yard and Main - fail. It ’ s Length is usually i - of the Length of the Mid - ship Beam.
MAIN - TOP - Its / ?, is one half of the Length of the Main - mast - and the T op - gall ant - m aft half the Length of the Main - top - mast.

mainourmancur.c: MAINOUR, Mancur, or Meinour, in a Le - gal Sense, signifies a Thing that aThieftaketh away, or stealth: As to be taken with the Mainour, is to be taken with the Thing stolen a - bout him.

mainpernable.c: MAINPERNABLE, is he that may be let to Bail. See the Statute of iVeftm.. cap.. made Anno A.. what Persons be mainpernable, and what not.

mainpernors.c: MAINPERNORS, are those Persons to whom a Person is delivered out of Cuft dy or Prison, and they become Security for him, either for Ap - pearance, or Satisfadion. They are called Ma - nucaptores, because they do as it were manu ca - per e & ducere captivum e custodia vel prison: And. the Prisoner is said to be delivered to Fail, from the Words of the Bail - piece, viz. A. B. &c. trade - tur in Ballium J. D. C ? R. R. &c.

mainprise.c: MAINPRISE, in our Law, signifies the taking or receiving a Man into Friendly Custody, that o - otherwise is or might be committed to Prison, up - on Security given for his Forth - coming at a Day assigned: And they that thus undertake for any, are called Mainpernors, ( which fee ) because they receive him into their Hands - whence also comes the Word Mainpernable, denoting him that may be thus bail ’ d: For in many Cafes a Man is not mainpernable whereof fee Bro. tit. mainprise per totum and F. N. B. sol.. When Mdnprifes may be granted, and when not, fee Cramp. Justice. of Peace, sol. and. And the Mirror of Justices says. That Pledges be those that bail or re - deem any thing but the Body of the Man j but Mainpernors are those that free the Body of a Man j and therefore that Pledges belong properly M A L to real and mix ’ d Actions, and Mainpernors to per - synal.

maintain.c: MAINTAIN R, is he thatfupports or seconds a Cause depending in Suit between others, either by disbursing Money, or making Friends for either Party, towards his Help.

maintenance.c: MAINTENANCE, is a Law Term, signify - ing the Ac t of a Maintainer, when he seconds a Cause depending between others: And when it is accounted Maintenance, and when not, fee Broke tit. Maintenance. The Writ that lies against a Man for this Offence, is also called Maintenance. MA ] OK - General, is an Officer in an Army, that receives the Generals Orders, and delivers them out to the Majors of the Brigades, with whom he concerts what Troops are to mount the Gaurd, what to go out upon Parties, what to form Detachments, or to be sent on Convoys, ( c. ’ Tis his Business also to view the Ground to encamp on, and he is next Subordinate to the General and Lieutenant - General.

major.c: MAJOR of a Brigade, eirherof Horse or Foot, is he that receives Orders, and the Word, from the Major - General, and gives them to the particular Majors of each Regiment. And the

MAJOR of a Regiment, is an Officer whose Business it is to convey all Orders to the Regi - ment; to draw it up, and to exercise it; to fee it march in good order, to look to its Quarters, and to rally it, if it happen to be broken in an En - gazement, ( c. He is the only Officer in a Regi - ment of Foot, that is allowed to be on Horse - back in Time of Service; but he is mounted, that he may speedily get from Place to Place, as Occasi - on serves. There is also in a Garrison an Of - ficer next to the Deputy - Governour, which is cal - led the Town
MAJOR, He ought to understand Fortificati - on, and hath Charge of the Guards, Rounds, Pa - troilles, and Sentinels.

majus.c: MAJUS - ? j, is a writ or Proceeding in some Customary Manours, in order to a Tryal of Right of Land.

make.c: MAKE. A Word frequently used by Lawyers, Signifying to Perform or Execute: As, to make his Law, is to perform that Law which he hath formerly bound himself to; that is, to clear him - self of an Action commenced against him by his Oath, and the Oaths of his Neighbours. To make Services or Customs, is nothing else but to perform them; and to make Oath, is to take Oath.

malacia.c: MALACIA, is a depraved Appetite, which covets those Things which are not fit to be eaten; also a Tenderness of Body. Blanchard.

malacticaorernollientia.c: MALACTICA, or Ernollientia, are Things which soften the Parts by a moderate Heat and Moisture, by dissolving some of them, and diffipa - ting others. Blanchard.

malagma.c: MALAGMA, the fame with Cataplasm; also tis used in the fame Sense as MalaStica.

malignusmorbus.c: MALIGNUS Morbus, a Malignant Disease, is that which rages more vehemently and continues longer than its Nature usually permits it to; do; as a Pestilential Fever, ( c.

malleable.c: MALLEABLE, that which will bear being hammered, and spread, being beaten. This Qua - lity belongs in the highest Degree to Gold, which is the molt duSlile or malleable of any Metal what - ever. Mr. Boyle reckons the Qualifications requi - lite to Malleableness, to be, Having the Corpu - scales, or Particles of such an adapted Size, Shape, and Figure, whether hooked, branched, ( c. that they can take fall hold of one another, and Rick so close, as to make the Body spread easily under the Hammer, and not break nor crack.

malleus.c: MALLEUS, is one of the Four little Bones id the Ear.

malleolusormalleuspedis.c: MALLEOLUS, or Malleus Pedis, is Two - fold: External i which is the lower Process at the foot of the Bone of the Leg, called Fibula or Internal, which is the lower Process of the Bone of the Leg, called Tibia: These make up or form the Ancle. Malleolus is alio used as a Term in Botany, for a Sprout that grows out of a Branch which grew out its self but the Year before. Columella.

malthacode.c: MALTHACODE, is a Medicine fofcened with Wax. Blanchard.

malummortuum.c: MALUM Mortuum, the Dead Disease, is a fort of Scab; so called, because it makes the Bo - dy appear black and mortified. It is in Colour Black, and inclining to Blue, and appears with a Crusty fort of Pimples, unseemly, and filthy, but without fending out Matter, or giving the Pati - ent Pain. It insects the Hips and Legs especially Blanchard.

mammillaryartery.c: MAMMILLARY Artery, or the Mammaria, is a Branch of the Arteries which supplies the Breads, and issues out pf the adjoining Trunk of the Aorta, as some lay; but more properly it ought to be said to come from the superiour Part of the Subclavian Branch of the Ascending Trunk of the Aorta,

mammamammilla.c: MAMMA, Mammilla, Vber, the Breads ] Duggs, ( c a The Grammarians call the inner Part Vber a, and the outward Protuberances Mam m z. The Subdance of the Breads is a white and soft Body, confiding internally of a Congeries of Conglomerated Glandules, by the means whereof the Milk is separated from the Arterious Blood, and is conveyed out by very little Pipes, which pals through the Nipples.

mammaryvessels.c: MAMMARY Vessels, are the Arteries and Veins that run through the Muscles and Glands of the Breads.

mammiformesprocejfus.c: MAMMIFORMES Procejfus, are the two Apo - phases of the Bone of the back - part of the Skull.

mandamus.c: MANDAMUS, is a Writ that lieth after the Year and Day; whereas in the mean time the Writ called Diem clausit extremum hath not been sent out to the Escheator for the fame Purpose to which it Ihould have been sent forth. See Diem clausit extremum. Mandamus, is also a Charge to the Sheriff, to take into the King ’ s Hands all the Lands and Te - onements of the King s Widow, that again her Oath formerly given, marryeth without the King ’ s Confenr.

mandate.c: MANDATE, is a Commandment of the King, or his Justices, to have any thing done for Dispatch of Judice; whereof you shall fee DU versify in the Table of the Regijler Judicial verbs Mandat um..

mandataryinlaw.c: MANDATARY, in Law, is he to whom & Charge or Commandment is given: Also he that obtains a Benefice by Mandamus.

mandiblila.c: MANDIBLILA, or rather Maxilla, the Jaw, is either Upper or Lower. The Upper Mandible con fids of Twelve Bones, on each side Six. The First is at the external Corner of the Eye, which joined with the Fore - process of the Bone of the Temples, produces the Jugal Bone, The Second condor / ate MAN ' MAR constitutes the inner Corner of the Eye, has a large Passage in it, by which the super - abunclant Moi - fture of the Eye descends to the Nostrils. The Third is within the Circle, of the Eye, interposed betwixt the other two. The Fourth, the greatest of all, forms the greatest Part of the Cheeks and the Palate and is elaborately contrived with p / oper Cavities for the Reception of the Teeth. The Fifth helps to make the Nose. The Sixth, with another Bone along with it, terminates the Extremity of the Palate. And all those are joi - ned rather by a plain Line than by Sutures. The Lower Jaw, at riper Years, grows into one conti - nued Bone, extreme hard and thick, and conse - quently very strong: It has two Processes, one A - cut, called Corone; the other in the Form of a little Head, called Ccndylus. It has two Holes within, and as many without, which make way for the Nerves: The Under Teeth are implanted in it, and is jointed with the inner side of the Bone of the Temples, called Os petrrfum. To these Twelve Bones, Columbus and Laurent ius are for adding a Thirteenth, which, they fay, liesbetween the innermost Space and the Os fpheroides, divi - ding the most inward Part of the Nostrils into two Parts, like a Septum; and therefore they call it Vomer. To these B. Ve fall us would have the Ossa fponglofa, which are in the innermost Ca - city of the Nose, to be added also,

manger.c: MANGER in a Ship, is a Circular Place made with Planks fattened on the Deck, right un - der the Hawses, being about a Foot and half in Height: The U fe of which is to catch and receive the Sea - water, beating in at the Hawses in a Stress of Weather.,.

mania.c: MANIA, a fort of Madness, is a Deprivation of Imagination and Judgment, with great Rage and Anger, but without a Fever; although a Fe - ver may be joined with a Mania proceeding from some other Cause.

manicahypocratis.c: MANICA Hypocratis, or Hypocrates his Sleeve, is a Woolen Sack, or Bag, in Form of a Pyramid ?; wherewith Aromatic f Wines, Medicines, and ma - ny other Liquors are strained. ’ Tis so called by the Chymists.

manipulus.c: MANIPULUS, is a Dry Measure, usual with Physicians in their Prefcriptions: For it is a de - terminate Quantity, to wit, as much as can be held in one Hand, meant for the most part of Herbs. Fa / ciculus is a different Quantity from Manipulus, an Handful; for it properly signifies an Armful. -..

manner.c: MANNER. A Word now much in use, which we have borrowed from the French Maniere. In Painting it signifies the Usage, Way, Mode, or Manner any Painter hath acquired, not only in the Management of his Hand or Pencil, but also as to his Obfervanee of the Three Principal Parts of Painting, Invention, Design, and Colour: And according as any one hath gotten a Habit or peculiar Way of Painting, we fay he hath such a Manner. If it be agreeable to the Rules of this Art, Natural, Strong, Easie, and Duly Proportioned, we fay ’ tis a Good manner; and if the Con - trary, a Bad manner. If he imitate any Famous Ancient Painter, as Much. Angelo, Raphael, &c. we lay He paints after their manner. So ’ tis alio in Scul - pure; and now adays in Singing, or Playing on any Instrument: When we would express our Ap - probation of any one ’ s Way of Singing or Flaying, we fay He hath a very Good manner.

MANNER; besides what hath been laid about Manner, I must take notice that they fay in Archi - texture, That an Order Heroically and Giganti - cally designed; where the. division of the principal Members. is put into a few parts; but those ha - ving all a bold and ample Relievo, is after the Grand Manner, As for example, in a Cor niche, if the Gola or Cimatium of the Corona; the Coping the Modillions or Dentelli make a noble appearance by the gracefulness of their ProjeCtures; and that we lee none of that ordinary Confusion which re - ' salts from thole little Cavities, quarter rounds of the Afiragal, and such little Ornaments as produce no effect in great and massy Works, and which do impertinently justle out the graceful and principal Members; then will the manner of this Corniche appear solemn and great, and approve it self to be performed after La Grand Maniere. In Mr. Eve - lyns Parallel of Ancient and Modern Architecture, Chap.. p.. you have a fine draught of this Grand Manner in an Ancient Dorick Pillar which was found at Albano joining to the Church of St. Mary near Borne.

mannopusaterm.c: MANNOPUS, a Term in the Common Law, signifying Goods taken in the Hand of an apple - bended Thief.

manor.c: MANOR, was a Noble fort of Fee granted partly to Tenants for certain Services to be per - formed, and partly reserved to the Uie of the Fa - mily, with Jurifditftion over his Tenants for their Farms: The whole Fee was termed a Lordjloip, of old a Barony; from whence the Court, that is always an Appendant to the Manor, is called the Court - Baron. Now a Aianor rather signifies the Jurisdiction and Royalty incorporeal, than the Land or Site: For a Man may have a Manor in gross, that is, the Right and interest of a Court - Baron, with the Perquifites thereunto belonging; and another, or others, have every Foot of the Land. But at this Day a Manor cannot be made, because a Court - Baron cannot now be made, and a Manor cannot be without a Court - Baron,

man.c: MAN - SLAUGHTER, is the unlawful killing of a Man, without prepensed Malice: As when two, that formerly meant no Harm one to another meet together, and upon some sudden Occasion falling out, the one killeth the other. It differed ! ' from Further, because it is not done with forego - ing Malice; and from Chance - medly, because it hath a present Intent to kill. And this is Felony, but admitted to the Benefit of the Clergy for the first time.
MAN - BOTE, was formerly a Recompence for Homicide, or a Pecuniary Compensation for oil - ling a Man.

manteletsinfortification.c: MANTELETS, in Fortification, are a kind of movable Pent - houses, and are made of pieces of Timber saw ’ d into Planks; which being about three Inches thick, are nail ’ d one over another to the Height of almost fix Foot. They are generally cased with Tin, and fet upon little Wheels, fothat in a Siege they may be driven before the Pioneers, and serve as Blinds, to shelter them from the Ene - mies Small - stion. There are also other forts of Mantelets, cover ’ d on the top, whereof the Miners make use to approach the Walls of a Town or Ca - ttle.

mantleinheraldry.c: MANTLE in Heraldry is that appearance of the Foldings of Cloth, Flouriihing, or Drapery, that is, in any Atchievement, drawn about a Coat of Arms: ’ Tis supposed to have formerly been the Representation of a Mantle of State in Blazon; ’ tis always said to be doubled, i. e, Lined throughout with one of the Furs, as Ermin, Pean, Verry, &c.

manucaptio.c: MANUCAPTIO, is a Writ that lies fora Man, who taken upon Suspicion of Felony, and offering sufficient Bail for his Appearance, cannot be ad - mitted thereto by the Sheriff, or other having Power to let to Mainprise.

manuschrifti.c: MANUS Chrifti, is a fort of Refined Sugar, so called, because it is put into Cordials for very weak People. Blanchard.

manutenentia.c: MANUTENENTIA, is a Writ used in case of Maintenance. See Maintenance.

map.c: MAP, is a Description of the Earth, or some par - dicular part thereof, projected upon a plain Super - socies; describing the form of Countries, Rivers, Situation of Cities, Hills, Woods and other Re - t ks

marasmodes.c: MARASMODES, is the Term for a Fever, which at last ends in a Consumption.

marcasite.c: MARCASITE, is the General Term for a Mineral Body, having in it some Metalline Parts; tho ’ many of them hold but a very little. Quantity of Metal. See Fojfils.

maritagio.c: MARITAGIO amijfo per defktam, is a Writ for the Tenant in Frank marriage, to recover Lands, &c. whereof he is divorced by another.

maritagioforisfa.c: MARITAGIO Forisfa & o., See Forfeiture of Marriage.

marline.c: MARLINE, is a small Line made ef Hemp un - twisted, that it may be the more gentle and pliable j its use is to sei e the ends of Ropes from sacring out: They use it also to seize the Straps at the Arse ( as they call it ) or lower end of the Block. Marling Sail; is, when being so rip ’ d out of the Bolt Rope, that it cannot be sewed in again, the Sail is fatten'd by Mar lint, put thro ’ the Eye - let holes made in it for that purpose unto the Bolt Rope.

marlinespikes.c: MARLINE Spikes, are small Spikes of Iron made for the Splicing together of small Ropes, and ais to open the Bolt Ropes when the Sails are sewed into them. They are only a kind of small Fiddj which fee.

marmorataaurium.c: MARMORATA Aurium, Ear - wax, is a certain Excrement of the Ear, laid there in the Auditory Passage from the openings of the Arteries, or Sweat out from the Cartilages.

marshal.c: MARSHAL: There be with us divers Officers of this Name, as Lord or Earl Marjhal of England, whose Office consists chiefly in matters of War and Arms, as well with us as in ether Countries. Alio, the Marjhal of the King ’ s House, whose spe - cial. Authority is in the King s Palace to hear and determine all Pleas of the Crown, and to punish faults committed within the Verge, and to hear and Judge of Suits between those of the King ’ s Hottlhold, &c. There be several other Officers of this Name, as Marjhal of the Just ices in Eyre; ' Marjhal of the Kjngs - Bench, who hath the Cufto - dy of the Kings - Bench Prison in South - wari: Ma - jhaloi the King ’ s - Hall, whose Office is, when the Tables are prepared,, to call out both those of the Houlhold, and Strangers, according to their ' Worth, and decently to place them, &c. Also Marjhal of the Exchequer, to whom the Court committeth the Custody of the King ’ s Debtors du - ring the Term time, for fecuring the Debts: He also affigneth Sheriffs, Efcheators, Cuftomers, and Collectors their Auditors, before whom they ( hall account.

marshalsea.c: MARSHALSEA, is the Court or Seat of the Marjhal of the King ’ s Houlhold, who formerly perhaps used to fit there in Judgment, or keep his Prison j and is now allowed for the Prison in South - VPdvf ( j

marsupialis.c: MARSUPIALIS feu Bufalis, is a Muscle of the Thigh, so called from its Tendons running through ( as it were ) a second fleshy Beginning of it self, which Duplication represents a Purse: It is also called Obturator Internus; it, ariseth broad and fleshy, from that part of the Os Ilium, Ischium, Pubis, and Ligament that inextended in the Great Foramen of the two last named Bones internally, and marches tranfverlly in the Sinus of the Ischium, ( fenced on each side by two Processes, the one Acute and the other Obtuse ) where it is externally Fleshy, but internally it hath three, sometimes four Tendons palling in so many distinct Furrows in the said Sinus, like so many Cords in a Quadruple Pulley, where it meets with the other fleshy begin - ning, commonly called its Mdrfupiuni, arising from the above - mentioned Acute and Obtuse Processes, which joyning with the said Tendons at their uni - ted Insertion to the Superior part of the oot of the great Trochanter, near the Implantation of the Fyrft formis: When this Muscle acteth, its Insertion is directed towards that part of the Ischium, over which its Tendons run after the manner of a Put - ley, and the Os Pernor is is thereby turned outwards.

martialregulus.c: MARTIAL Regulus. of Antimony See Regulus. When any Particles are said to be of a Martial Nature in Chymistry or Natural Philosophy, tis meant, that they partake of the Nature of Iron or Steel. The Chymifts calling Iron, Mars.

martiallaw.c: MARTIAL Law, is the Law of War, depend - ding upon the King ’ s Pleasure, or his Lieutenant; For the King in time of Peace, never makes any Laws, but by common Consent in Parliament, yet in War he useth absolute Power insomuch that his Word is a Law; but even this Power hath of late Years been in verted in the King, or his Gene - rals of the Army by Aft of Parliament, and under particular Reftriftions too. Read the new Adis of Parliament for punilhifig Mutineers and Defer - ters f

martlettheterminheraldry.c: MARTLET the Term in Heraldry for a Pid - geon, with its Feet erased or torn off - ’ tis also the Difference, or markofDiftindtion in an Escutcheon for the fourth Brother or Family.

martnets.c: MARTNETS in a Ship, are small Lines fatten - ed to the Leetch of the Sail, being Reeved thro ’ a Block on the Topmast - head, and fother comedown by the Matt to the Deck. Those Martnets which belong to the Top - fails are fattened ( after the feme way ) to the Heads of the Top - gallant Matts, but their Fall comes down no farther than the Top, when it is haled: The Word is Top the Martnets j i. e. Hale them up. Their design is, in furling the Sail, to bring that part of the Leetch which is next the Yard Arm, close up to the Yard, that so the Sail may sure up the closer.

marsthename.c: MARS, the Name of one of the Planets which moves round the Sun in an orbit between that of the Earth and Jupiter. To view this Planet, there requires a good Te - lefcope, with small Apertures on the object - glass, or else his Glairy Light makes but a confused Ap - pearance. This Planet as ( well as the reft ) borrows its Light from the Sun; and has its Increase and De crease of Light like the Moon and it may be seer almost biffefted when in his Quadratures with the Sun, or in his Perigaon, but never corniculated or falcated as the other Inferiors. Mar eh.. Dr. Hoop observed this Pla - net, with a foot Tube, and few its Body as large very near as the Moon at Full; and in it he observed several Spots, and particularly a Tri - angular one which having a motion, he conclu - ded the Planet to have a turbinated Motion round its Centre. In the Year. February the th in the Morning, Mr. Caffini with a foot Telescope, observed two dark Spots in the first: Face of Mars, moving frory / i at Night until Break of Day, February the th in the Evening, he few two Other Spots in the other Face of this Planer, like those of the first, but much bigger: And conti - ning the Observations, he found the Spots of these two Faces to turn by little and little from East to Weft, and to return at the space of Hours, Minutes, to the feme situation, where - in they were seen at first. Whence he concluded, That the Revolution, of this Planet round its Axis, is perform ’ d in the space of Hours, Minutes, or there - bouts The Distance of Mars from the Sun, is about one and an half of that of the Earth from the Sun -, and therefore to an Eye placed in Mars, the Diameter of the Sun would appear by one and an half less than it doth to us, and conse - quently his Light and Heat will be but half of what it is here on our Earth but this admits of a sensible Variation, because of the great Eccen - trinity of Mars his Orbit, yet not so great as in Mercury. Mars his Year is almost twice as long as ours, and his Natural Day a little greater than purs but his Artificial Day, or the Time in which the Sun appears above his Horizon ( besides the Two - light before Sun - rife, and after Sun - fet, accord - ing to the Daily height of the Atmosphere, ) is al - most every where equal to his Night and con - sequently in one and the fame place on his Sur - face there can be but little variety of Seasons as to Summer and Winter, &c. the Reason of which is, That the Axis of the Diurnal Revolu - tion of this Planet, is nearly at Right Angles with the Plane of the Orbit. But Places situate in divers Latitudes, or at divers Distances from his Equator, will have very different Degrees of Heat, by reason of the differe'nt Indication of the Suns Rays to the Horizon as is the Case of our Earth when the Sun is in the Equi - noxes. And from hence, the Learned Dr. Gregory in his Afiren. Phyfi & Geometr. p., conjectures very probably, That the Fascia of this Planet do arise: which are certain Swathes or Fillets which appear in Mars, and are posited parallel to his E - quator. For since there is always in the fame Climate ( here ) nearly the fame Degree of Hear, hris likely that these Spots in Mars owing their original to Heat and Cold, ( as in our Earth Clouds and Snow do ) may be extended in the said Cli - mates in parallels to the Equator, or to the Circle of Mars his Diurnal Revolution, and so form the Fascia. And the fame is true of Jupiter, which, as well as Mars, hath a Perpetual Equinox. That Mars hath an Atmosphere, like ours, is argued from the Phenomena of the Fix ’ d Star ’ s appearing obfcur ’ d and as it were extindr, when they are seen just by the Body of Mars: And if so, a Spectator in Mars will hardly ever fee Mer - cury, unless it may be in the Sun when that Pla - net passes over his Disk like a Spot, as he doth sometimes to us. To an Eye in Mars, Venus will appear about as far from the Sun, as Mercury doth from him with us and the Earth, as far as Venus appears to us, to be from the Sun. And when the Earth, being seen from Mars, appears in Conjun & ion with, and very near to the Sun, the Martial Spedator will fee that which Caffini once or twice saw in Venus, vi. The lower Planet ( or the Earth ) appear horned or falcated; and its Sa - stellite, the Moon of the fame Figure, and at its greatest distance, not above Minutes of a De - gree from the Earth. Greg. Ajironom.

marshallingacoatofarms.c: MARSHALLING, a Coat of Arms ( in He - raldry ) signifies the due and proper joining of fe - Veral Coats of Arms in one and the fame Shield or Escutcheon, together with their Ornaments, Parts and Appurtenances.

mascleaterm.c: MASCLE, a Term in He - raldry for a bearing of this Fi - gure: Gules a Chevron Ermim between three Mascle s Argent, by the Name of Bellgrave. Guillim faith, the Mascle rere - fents the Malli of a Net and is an honourable Bearing. A Mascle differs from a Lozenge, only by being voided.

masse.c: MASSE, this Word is used by the Natural Phi - lofophers to express the Quantity of Matter in a - ny Body, and this Sir If. Newton faith, he found by most accurate Experiments on Pendulums, to be always proportionable to the Weight of Bo - dies, which is a good Argument to prove the Necessity of allowing a Disseminate Vacuum.

massetersinanatomy.c: MASSETERS in Anatomy, are. short thick Tendinous Muscles of the lower Jaw -, produced forwards from the Os Primum of the Upper Jaw, and backwards from the Jugal Bone they are conceded to the Lower Jaw. They assist the Temporal es to move it to the right - side, left side, and forward according to the various Disposition of the Fibres.

master.c: MASTER of the Bolls, is an Assistant to the Lord Chancellor, or Lord Jfeeper of the Great Seal of England, in the High Court of Chancery, and in his Absence, hears the Causes there, and gi - veth Orders. He is by some called, Clerk, of the Bolls. And he has the disposing of the Offices of the Six Clerks, Clerks of the Petty Bag, Ex - miner of the Court, and Clerks of the Cha - pel.

MASTER of the Mint. - In the second Year of H.. that was the Title of him that now is called the Warden of the Mint, whose Office it is to re - weive the Silver and Bullion that comes to the Mint to be coined, and to take care thereof.

MASTER of the Court of Wards and Liveries was the chief Officer and Judge of that Court of Wards, kept the Seal of it, and was named and assigned by the King. But this Court and all its. Officers, Members, Power, and Appurtenances, is taken away by a Statute made the th of Car. X C a rZ. e
MASTER of the Horse, hath ' the Rule and Charge of the King ’ s Stable: This Officer is very Honourable, and usually a Nobleman, is men - tioned in Eli.. and E...

MASTER of the Posts, was an Officer of the King ’ s Court that had the appointing, placing and displacing of all such as provided Post - Horses to carry the King ’ s Meffages and other Business. He also was to pay them their Wages, &c. This Of - ficer is mentioned in ied... but now by a Statute made Car.. c.. he is appointed by the King ’ s Letters Patent, with Rates and Rules prescribed in the said A St.
MASTER of the Armory, is an Officer verse tioned Elis '. c.. and hath the case of the King ’ s Armour in any hanging Armories; with power of putting in and out all Inferiour Offi - cers.

MASTER of the Jewel House, is mentioned in Elis. c.. and is an Officer of the King ’ s Household of great Credit Being allowed Bcuge of Court, that is, Diet for himself and the Clerks of the Office, and hath a Lodging in the Court. He hath charge of all the Gold and Silver Plate used at the King ’ s Table, or belonging to any Of - ficer of account attending the Court and of all Plate remaining in the Tower of London, as also. of Chains and loose Jewels not fix ’ d to any Gar ment.

MASTER of the Household. This Officer is called Grand Mafier, &c. and Lord Steward of the Kings Household in H... And in the first of Q. M. and ever since he is called Lord Stew - ard, &c and under him there is a principal Offi - cer called by this Name of the Mafier of the House - hold. s -
MASTER of the Ordnance, mentioned E - U.. and is a great Officer, to whose care all the King ’ s Ordnance and Artillery is committed.
MASTER of the Faculties, is an Officer under the Archbishop of Canterbury, who grants Licences and Difpenfations he is mentioned in the Statute of laying Impofitions at Law of, Car..

masters.c: MASTERS of the Chancery, are Assistants in Chancery to the Lord Chancellour, or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, in Matters of Judgment. Of these there are some Ordinary, some Extraordi - nary of Ordinary there are twelve, ( whereof the Mafier of the Bolls is accounted one ) whereof some fit in Court every Day in each Term, and have referred to them ( at the Lord Chancellor, Lord Keeper, or AJ after of the Bolls Discretion ) Interlocutory Orders, for starting Accounts, com - putting Damages, and the like taking of Oaths, Affidavits, and Acknowledgments of Deeds and Recognizances. The Extraordinary do ACt in all the Country Ten Miles from London, by ta - king Recognizances and Affidavits, Acknow - lodgment f Deeds, &c. for, the ease of the Sub - ject.

masticationorchewing.c: MASTICATION, or Chewing, is an ACtion, ' whereby we break and divide the Meat into small pieces with our Teeth, and mix it with the Spittle or Saliva, in order to its being the more easily fermented, digested, and turned into Chyle in the Stomach.

mastigatories.c: MASTIGATORIES, are Medicines which are designed to provoke Spitting. By some they are called Apophlegmations.

mastoideiinanatomy.c: MASTOIDEI, in Anatomy is the fame with Mammillares, and are such Processes any where, as are like Breasts or Dugs, which from a broad Basis, end in an obtuse top, and are shaped like the Teats in a Cows - Udder. This Name is given by some Writers to those Muscles which, bend the Head proceeding from the Neck - bone and the Breast - bone, terminating in the Process Mammiformis. These Muscles a - rife partly tendinous, and partly fleshy, from the upper part of the Os Pectoris near half the Cla - vice mat vice z with two seemingly distinct Originations. Mr. Cowper faith, When either of these Mmcles ad, they turn the Face to the contrary side. The Pro - ofs, or Apophysis of the Os Temporale, which is m shape something like the Teats of A Cow, is cal - led by this Name and so are the Processes of the Qlfattory Nerves..

masts.c: MASTS of a Ship are the Main - mail, Main top - mail, Main - top - gallant - mail, Fore - mail, Fore - tap - mail, Fore - top - gallant - mail, Mizen - mast, and Mizentop - mast; amongst which, may alio be reckoned her Boltiprit; all which fee. For the Proportions of Mails, Sir H. Manwa - ring gives these Rules. Whatever the Breadth of a Ship be in Feet, multiply of that Breadth by, the Product is the Length of her Main - mast in Yards. Thus if a Ship be foot at the Midjhip Beam, i of is Therefore that Ships Main - mail must be Yards, or feet in Length. Then for its bigness he allows an Inch to every Yard in length; and therefore this Main - mail must be Inches thro ’ or thick. The Fore - mast of a Ship must be r of the Length of the Main - mail, that is in this case, Yards, or Feet i; Thick or thro ’, it must be near In The Boltfprit or Bowfpnt, is always the fame length and bigness with the Fore - mast. And the Mi en - mast must be just half the length of the Main - mast, and half as thick.

materdura.c: MATER Dura, called also Dura Meninx, is a Membrane which sticks close to the Skull within, in some places, and mediately covers both the Brain and Cerebellum;. it has four Cavities which supply the place of the Veins, and come together betwixt the Brain and Cerebellum, which Conjun - ction is called T ocular.

matertenuis.c: MATER Tenuis, ot Pin Meninx, is a Membrane which immediately clothes the Brain and Cerebel - lum - is eXtreamly full of Sanguinary Vessels, and is design d, as some think, to keep in the Spirits generated in the Brain and Cerebellum, that they ly not away.

materiamedica.c: MATERIA Medica, is whatever is us d in the Art of Medicine for the Prevention or Cure of Dis - eafes, whether colledcd or prepared from Plants, Animals, Minerals, &c. by Chymifty, or Pharmacy.

mathematicks.c: MATHEMATICKS, originally signifies any Discipline or Learning, ( udfans ) but now tis pro - perly, that Science which teaches or contemplates whatever is capable of being Numbered or Mea - fured, as it is computable or measurable. And that Part of Mathematicks which relates to Number only, is call ’ d Arithmetic: That which relates to Measure in general, whether Length, Breadth, Motion, Force, &c. is called Geometry. Mathematicks may be reckon ’ d either, . Pure, Simple, or AbfiraBed, which considers abftradled Quantity, without any Relation to Mat - ter, or Sensible Objects Or, . Mixt Mathematicks, which is interwoven e - very where with Physical Considerations. Mathematicks alio is divided into Speculative, which proposes only the simple Knowledge of the thing proposed, and the bare contemplation of Truth or Falfhood. And Practical, which teaches how to demonstrate something useful, or to perform something that shall be proposed for the Benefit and Advantage of Mankind.
