metal.c: METAL C APT U, and Metacarpium, is the Back of the Hand, made of Four oblong little Bones, which expand the Palm of theHand, and they are called Pofl - brachialia. ME ACARPUS, is a. Bone of the Arm, ma. de up of Four Bones which are annexed ' to the Four Fingers; that which sustains the Fore - finger is the biggest and longed. They are round and long, a little convex and round towards the Back of the Hand, and concave and plain to - wards the Palm: They are hollow in the mid - dle, and full of Marrow; they touch one ano - ther only at their Extremities, leaving Spaces in their middle, in which lie the Mufculi inter off ei. In the upper end there is a Sinus, which receives / the Bones of the Wrist, and their lower Extre - mity is round, and is received into the Sinus of the first Bones of the Fingers.

METAL, a word frequently used about a Piece of Ordnance, or Great Gun: The Out - ride or Surface of her is called, the Superficies of her Metals: When the Mouth of a Great Gun lies lower than her Breech, they fay, She lies un - der Metal; but if she lies truly level, Point - blank, or right with the Mark, they fay, She lies right with her Metal.

metacondyli.c: METACONDYLI, are the utmost Bones of the Fingers.

metalsandminerals.c: METALS and Minerals. The Excellent Pro - mater of all useful Learning, Bishop Wilkins, in. his Real Character, gives the following Table of Metals. Metal is a Mineral, for the most part of a Hard Conjiflence, Close, Dudtile, and Fusil; and may be diftinguJfked into L PerfeEll And this is either, ’ LFactitiouS. II. Imperfects With Reference to gjndt'm, Lfiecrementitious Parts. ( /. First, Natural Metals are such as of themselves grow in the Earth, without any kind of Mixture or other help by the Art of Men. And these are either, ' i. More Rare and Precious. Of a Tellowifh Colour, most heavy not growing in particular Mines, where it is debased with any droplie Mixture, but, found pure either in small Sands, of rocky Branches ' and this is Gold. Whitish Colour, next in Value to Gold, not lubjecft to Rust, yielding ( when fttuckj a pleasant Sound; as Silver; ' v i r . Of a Middle Value, and of a Whitish Colour, and more soft Confidence, as Tin: Or of a Reddijh Colour, as Copper. . Of a Baser Value, and more Common, " - are Lead, which is of a yet softer Confidence., darkjjh Colour, and not Sonorus. Iron, which is of an hard Confidence, dnd of rusty dark Colour too. B V ‘ / Secondly, Factitious Metals, are luch as are made by the Art of Man: Of which some are made of Copper, and Lapis Calaminaris, as Brass. Stone of T in, Lead, and T in - Glass, as Pewter. Or of iron depurated, by frequent heating, and beat - ing, and boiling with Salts as St & el. ( Thirdly, Imperfect JKfnds of Metal, are either Fluid, as Mercury or Quickfiher. - Or i Solid and Confident. And some of these are used for Purging, and chiefly upwards, as Antimony. Some are used for making of Pewter, being of a sinning brittle Substance, as Bismuth or T in - Glass. Others are used for making of Solder, as Spelter, or Spalt. And some are made use for Painting, as Cinnabar, Vermilion, and Black, Lead. Fourthly, Recrementitious Parts of Metals, are such as are cast off either in the Preparation of them by Melting; as Litharge, which is a kind of Scum arising from the Purification of Silver from Lead and Spodium and Pompholix, which fly out from Copper when it is in Fusion, and either fall down again to the Ground, as the former, or adhere to the Roof or Walls, as th latter: Or else they come from the Metal by Beating or Hammering, as the Scoria, or Scales or ar'ife from Corruption either in the general way, as Rujl, or after a particular manner, as in the ma - king of Verdigreafe and Ceruse one from Copper, or Brass, and the other from. ead. But notwithstanding this Scheme be a good general Summary yet a goad Discourse on this - Subject is very much wanting and indeed to do it well, will be a very difficult Task: Because in the Mineral Kfngdom ( as Tit. Woodward ob serves in his Excellent Natural History of the Earth, Part. ) there is nothing Regular, Constant, or Certain: Neither Colour, Figure, nor their Place or Situation in the Earth, are to be trusted to, or relief upon, so as positively to make any Judgment from thence. A common Marchafte, or Pyrites, shall have the Colour and Brightness of Gold or Silver, and yet afford nothing but a little Sulphur and Vitri - ol whilst another Body, having only the Refem - balance of a Pebble or a Stone, shall have a plenty - ful Admixture of a valuable Metal in it. Nothing is more common than to find the fame Metal shot also into very different Forms and Figures as well as to find different kinds of Metal of the fame Form and Figure: And a Bo - dy which hath the slape and appearance of a Di - among, may prove upon examination, to be no - thing but Chrystals of Selenites nay, perhaps on - ly common Salt, or Alum, naturally Chryftalliz ’ d, r ! shot into that Form ? So also as to their Place in the Earth, there is the fame uncertainty l Sometimes we find them in the Perpendicular Fissures, or Intervals of the Strata sometimes interspersed in the Bodies of the Strata, and sometimes in both: Only indeed in the Gems ther is this difference, That the T ? pa es, Amethifts, Emerals, cc. which grow in the Fissures, ari ordinarily Chryftallized or ffiot ' into Angular Figures, whereas those found in the Strata, are in rude Lumps, only like so ma - ny Yellow, Purple, or Green Pebbles not but that even these that are thus lodged in the Strata ' are also sometimes found Chryftallized, and in the Forms of Cubes, Rhombs, &c. but then those found in the Strata, ate easily diftinguiflied from the other, because they are without their Rpo ( as the Jewellers call it ) or the Abruptness at their ' Ends, whereby the others adhere to the Stone or Sides of the Intervals, which Abruptness is oc - cafioned by their being broken off from thence And those which are found inclosed in solid Stone, Marble, &c. being difficultly separable from the Stony Matter which adheres to them on all sides, have commonly some of that Matter sticking to them on all their sides; whereby they are diftinguiflied from those found in the Perpen - dicular Intervals, they adhering only by one End, as was above observed. The fame Metals are alio placed indifferently in all kind of Terrestrial Matter, or in Strata of very different Natures. They are frequently al - so variously intermixed one with another so that ’ tis a rare thing to find any of them Pure and Simple, but Copper and Iron shall be in the fame Mass, Gold and Copper, Silver and Lead, Tin and Lead - yea, sometimes all the Six toge - ther in one and the fame Lump. ’ Tis the fame thing with Minerals and Mine - rals and Metals are very often Blended and Inter - mixed together. Now the knowledge of this may be of good use to undeceive those, who by reading of some Authors, are persuaded, That all things relating to Metals and Minerals, are tranfaded by Na - ture, in a most regular and Accurate Order, whereas indeed there is nothing like that and the only Landing Ted, and diftinguifliing Cha - ra & eristic of any Metal or Mineral, must be fought for in the Constituent Matter of it, and it must first be brought down to that, before any cer - tain Judgment can be given of it. Those Metals and Minerals which are reposit - ted in the Bodies of the Strata, are either found there in Grains, or small Particles, or else amaf - fed into Balls, Lumps, or Nodules which No - rules are either of an irregular and uncertain Fi - gure, as the common Pyritce, Flints, Agates, Onyxes, Pebbles, Cornelians, Jafpers, &c. or else they are of a Figure somewhat regular and ob - fervable as the Belemnites, the fe veral forts of Mineral Coral, the Stelechites, the Lapis Mucetoi - des, vulgarly called, Fungites: The Afiroites, or Starry Stone as well that fort with the prominent, as that with the Concave Stars: The Selenites, the Echinated Chrystalline Balls, with many more ' Analogous Bodies. Those which are contained in the Perpendicular Intervals of the Strata, are either such as are there gathered into a Rude Heap, without any particular Form or Order, lying included within the two opposite Walls or Sides of the said Inter - vals, M E T vals, which, according to their quantity, they wholly, or partly fill. In inch manner is Sparr, and other Minerals usually found; as also the common Ores of Lead, Tin, Iron, and other Metals: Or else such as are distinguishable by being of some observable Fi - gure; as the Sparry Stir ice or Iceycles, called Sta - lactate, or rather Stagoniu; the Native Saline Iceycles, or Salt Stalaclitum; the Vitriolum Stala - cticum Nathum; the Vitriolum Capillare; the Alu - men Stala'ditum and Capillare; Miner a Ferri Sta - laftica, which when several of the Cylindrick Sti - rice are Contiguous, growing together, as it were, in one Sheaf, is called Brujh Iron Ore; the Ar - gentum Arborefcens and Capillare. To these add also the chryftiallized Ores and Minerals, vig. The Tin, and Mundick Grains, the Iron Rhombs, chyftallized Nitre, Salt, Alum, Vitriol, and Sul - pour: Of which fort alio, are the Gems or Stones that are here ftrat into Cubes, into Pyramidical Forms, or into Angulated Columns; consisting of fix Sides, and mucronated or terminating in a Point; being either Opake or Pellucid, or but part - ly so, and coloured Black, White, Grey, Red, Purple, Blue, Yellow, or Green: v. gr. Chrystal, the Pseudo - Adamantes, the Cornish and Brifiol - Stones, Cryjl allied Spans, the Iris, the Ametbyfi, the Saphire, the T pag, the Emerald, cc. As to the Origin and Production of Metals and Minerals, the Dr. from the Light his Obfer - nations have given him, comes to these Conclu -. signs. i. That the far greatest part of our Metals and Minerals, vi. all iuch as are now found, in the Strata, do owe their present Frame and Or - der to the ZJniverfal Deluge, when the Strata of Stone, Earth, Marble, themselves were also formed. At which Time also were all Metallick and Mineral Nodules whatsoever formed; as well those in Rude Lumps, such as the common Pyri - tae, Flints, Pebbles, Agates, Onyxes, Jafpers, Corne - tions, See. as those of a more observable Figure and regular Shape, as the Selenites, Belemnites, Ste - lechites, Mineral Coral. z. That the Metallick and Mineral Matter now found in the Perpendicular Intervals or Sis - fures of the several Strata, of which the Body of the Earth is composed, was all of it originally, and at the time of the Deluge, lodged in the Bodies of those Strata, that it was educed thence and transmitted into these Intervals line that time; the Intervals themselves not existing till the Strata were formed, and afterwards broken, to let the Water from off the Earth. See Part z. Corfctt.,. and Part.. Sett. z. of his Natural History of the Earth. But he supposes that the Water which is continually ascending from the Abyss, towards the Surface of the Globe, ( fee Abyss, and the word Springs ) continually pervading the Bodies of the Strata, detaches out of their Pores and Interfti - ces, such Metallick and Mineral Corpuscles as lie loose in its way, ( and which are withal so small as to be capable of pasting thro ’ those Interstices ) forcing them along with it to the Perpendicular Intervals; where having more room, and a freer passage than before, it deserts them and leaves them in those Intervals; and that this way all the Mineral and MetaHick Metal now found in tho e Places was brought thither, - and there do still grow and increase. But that these in the Strata do not, nor cannot grow, but on the contrary, are continually leR fened and diminished, by so much as hath been conveyed into their Perpendicular Intervals, and hath been brought forth on the Surface of the Earth by Springs, Rivers and Exhalations from the Abyss, ever since the Deluge. The Dodtor supposes also, that the Bitumen, which is found in Lumps, or coagulated Mattes, in some Springs - and which in others, is found floating on the Surface of the Water in the Form of an Oyl, ( Tailed by Naturalists, Naphtha and Petroleum: ) That the Salt wherewith the Salima or Salt Springs abound, the Vitriol, Alum, Nitre Sulphur, Sparr, and other Minerals, wherewith the AciduLe, or Medicinal Springs are impregn - ted; all these Minerals, he faith, were first long - ed in the Strata of Stone, Coal, Earth, &c. and have since been educed thence, and conveyed in - to those Springs, by the Water pervading those Strata in its passage from the Abyss towards the said Springs. See a much larger Account of this Matter under the word Fojfils.

metallurgy.c: METALLURGY, is the Working or Operas tion upon Metals, in order to render them most fine, hard, bright, beautiful, serviceable or useful to Mankind.

metapedium.c: METAPEDIUM, the fame in the Foot, that Metacarpus is in the Hand.

metaphoratropeinrhetoric.c: METAPHOR, a Trope in Rhetoric, by which we put a strange and remote Word for a proper Word, by reason of its resemblance with the thing of which we speak: As a King is called the Head of his Kingdom, because he commands the Members of the Politick Body, as the Head does the Natural Body.

metaphrenum.c: METAPHRENUM, is that part of the Back, which comes after the Diaphragm. Blanchard.

metaptosis.c: METAPTOSIS, is the regenerating of one Disease into another, as of a Quartan Ague, into a Pertain; and on the contrary, of an Apoplexy into a Pa ! fie, &c.

metastasis.c: METASTASIS, is when a Disease goes from one part to another; which happens to Apople & ick People, when the Matter which affeefts the Brain is mandated to the Nerves.

metatarsus.c: METATARSUS, is composed of five little Bones, connected to those of the first ' part of the Foot, which immediately succeeds the Leg.

meteors.c: METEORS, ( according to the Cartesians ) are certain various Impreffions made upon the Ele - ments, exhibiting them in different Forms, and are called Meteors from their Elevation; because for the most part, they appear to be high in the Air, and they are either Fiery, Airy, or Wa - tery. Fiery Meteors, are such as consist of; a Fat, Sulphurous kindled Smoak, whereof there are several kinds; as Ignis Fatuus, Trans, Ignis Py - ramidal is, Draco Volans, Capra Saltans, Thunder and Lightning, &c. Airy Meteors, are such as consist of Flacuous land Spiritous Exhalations, as Winds, &c. ’ E a Watery M I C Watery Meteors, consist of Vapours, or Watery Particles, by the Action of Heat separated from each other, and variously modified, as main, Dew, See. Dr. Woodward, in his Natural History of the Earth, p. zo. supposes the Matter of Meteors to be in good measure of a Mineral Nature; and that the Mineral Particles contained in the Strata of the Earth, are raised up by the Subterranean Heat or Fire, along with the Vapours ascending from the Abyss, and pervading thole Strata, and especially at such times as the Sun ’ s Power is so great, as to penetrate the exterior Parts of the Earth, and therefore help to mount them up into the Atmosphere. These Sulphurous, Nitrous, and other light and active Mineral Particles do form Meteors in the Air, and particularly are the Cause of Thunder and Lightning, See. and other Fiery Compositions there.

methodordisposition.c: METHOD, or Disposition, is that Action of the Mind, by which we range various Ideas, Judgments and Ratiocinations upon one and the lame Suhjedt, in that order which is most proper for its Explanation; and a right Method of Enqui - ry after Truth, or the Prosecution of any Demon - Itration will be found to consist also in a Regular Train of Arguments and Consequences rightly disposed in their just and Natural Order. If you will believe Des Cartes, he faith, in his Book De Method, That he was able to master the greatest Depths in Geometry, by only observing constantly these four following Rules in his Studies. First, never to admit any thing for Truth, and to treasure it up in the Mind as such, unless we be demonstratively allured, that it is such. Secondly, To divide the Difficulties of the Pro - blem, or Matter enquired after, into such a pro - per Number of Parts, as is most convenient for its Resolution. Thirdly, To observe exadl Order and Method in our Thoughts and Enquiries, so as to begin with the plainest and ealieft things first, and then to proceed on gradually to things more and more difficulty Fourthly, To be sure not to flip, overlook, or omit any thing either in the Difficulties to be sol - yed, or in the Means of Enquiry. These are indeed very good Rules, and I question not were very serviceable to him in his Geometrical Enquiries; but the Sight of our Countryman Harriot ’ s Algebra, did him as much Service as all of them. In Mathematical Enquires, there are two gent - ral Methods commonly made use of, the Analyti - cal, and the Synthetical; which fee: And to which may be added, The etical and Porifii - cal Methods; which you will find under these Words.

metonicktear.c: METONICK Tear, or Period, is the space of Years; in which time, the Lunations return, and happen as they were before; ’ tis sometimes called, The Great Metonick. Tear, and is the fame with the Cycle of the Moon.

metonymyortranfncmination.c: METONYMY, or Tranfncmination, ( a Fi - gure or Trope in Rfetorick. ) is the putting of one Name for another, or expressing a thing by ano - ther Name, than which properly belongs to it as if we Ihould fay, All the World reads Cicero, Cadar ravaged the Gauls: It would be plain ’, what we intended, That the World reads CiceroV Workj, Cxfar ’ s Army ravaged ' the Gauls.

metopainarchitecture.c: METOPA, in Architecture, is the Interval or Space between every Triglyph in rhe Prize of the Dorick, Order. The Ancients used to adorn these Parts with Carved Works or Paintings, re - presenting the Heads of Oxen, Vessels, Bafons, and divers other Instruments that were used in their Sacrifices.

micrometer.c: MICROMETER, is an Instrument made of Brass, being a Movement with a Plate, or Face divided like a Clock or Watch, with an Index or Hand, which ( being turned ) moves two Aiding Plates of Brass with Hairs, and counts on the Plate the Revolves or Turns of the endless Screw. This Instrument is fitted to a large Telescope, and used in Aftrencmy, to find the Diameters of the Stars, or Planets. The Description of this Instrument of Mr Town - ley, improved by Dr. Hook., you may fee more at large in Philofoph. Tran fa cl. N.. and the Uses in, N.. See Vol. II.

microscope.c: MICROSCOPE, is an Optical Instrument, which by extreamly magnifying ( as they fay ) any Object, helps us to discover the minute Par - titles of which Bodies are composed, and the cu - rious Frame and Contexture of them. To make very small Jingle Eye - glasses for Microscopes. Get some very small Silver - wire, and double it up and down like a Skin of Thread, in order to make a Wiek ( for a Lamp ) of a moderate size; then fill a Lamp with Spirit of Wine, well dephlegmated, and use the Silver - wire instead of a Cotton - wiek: Then having ready some fine Glass beaten, powdered, and lifted very small, and well washed and dried, take some of it on the point of a Silver Needle filed very small, and witted a little with Spittle, and holding it in the Flame of the Lamp, turn it about till it melt, ( as it will soon do ) into a fine round Globule: You must hold it in the Flame no longer than till it come to its round Figure, left you burn it: The only difficulty is in giving it that Roundness exactly, bur Practice will soon learn you the knack of it; they must be cleansed afterwards by rubbing them a while on soft Leather. The best Glasses of this kind that ever I law, are made by the above mentioned Mr. Mellen, who formerly lived in Abchurch - Lane. In Philof. Tranfabi. N.. is an account of a Microscope of Eujlach. He uses, instead of a common double Convex Eye - glass, two Plane Convex ones, which are so placed as to touch one another in the mid - dle of their Convex Surface. By which means the Glass will take in more of any Object, will re - present it flat and not crooked, and will magnifie also ( as they call it ) very much. This Glass had / our several Lengths ( made by Draws ); at the least Length, which was Inches, it magnified Lines times bigger than they appear to the naked Eye j at the second Length times; at the third Length times; at the fourth Length. As to the Method of making the fame Glass magnifie differently, at different Lengths Mr. Mar / hall hath brought it to bear very well in his ( mall Pocket Microscopes; and this I take to be a good Improvement, which he hath added to the Glasses of Campani, which are made after that manner, but with only one Degree of Magnifying with one and the fame Glass. There is an Ac - count of several Microfcopical Experiments, by One Mr. Stephen Gray; where he speaks of making Microscopes with a Globule of Water only, put into an Hole made in a small Brass Plate, which I my self have often tried; and were it not for the trembling Motion of the Fluid, it would do very well. He faith also, That by applying a small Globule ofPepper Water, &c. to his bare Eye, ( i. e. by fix - I ing it on the Surface of his Eye ) he could, in a darkened Room, by Candle - light, or Moon - light, or by looking thro ’ a small Hole in. a piece of Pa - per, discern the Animalcula which were in it, ex - ceedingly magnified; and oftentimes, when the drop of the Fluid was round and well defined, Very distend and plain. Thus, for in - stance, If you use the Objecft - Glass, or ( either of which will shew the Circulation of the Blood ) you must fix the upper Edge of the Collar E. at the Mark or on the Pillar. And then will the Microscope be very near its exact distance from the Objedfc j so that by a small turn or two of the Nut I. ei - ther way, you may soon exactly fit it to your own Eye, and place the Object in its true di - ftintft Basis. By this Microscope, Liquors also may be very dommodioufiy Examined j for if you place a small drop of any Liquor on the Glass - plate just in the middle of the spot of Light ( c ), the parts of it will become very visible, and its Animalcula, if it have any, will be discovered. And thus may the Eels In Vinegar, the small Creatures in Black - Pepper - water, or in Waters where Wheat, Barly, ( fic. bath been Infused, the Eels and other small li - ving Creatures in Puddle - water, be as plainly seen as by almost any other Micro / cope. And one thing I ought not to omit to speak on this occasion; which is, That I have often with this Glass, seen the Circulation of the Blood in the Fins of the Tail of Tadpoles; and indeed more conspicuously here than in any other Creature: For the Fins growing all round the Tail, and coming but a little way out beyond the Body of It, both the Ejaculation of the Blood out by the Arteries, and its return again by the Veins, is much quicker than in the Tails of Fishes j and a - abundance more Streams, turns and windings of the moving Blood are here visible, than I could ever see in any other Animal. To which I may add, That the Creature will live a good while out of the Water, and will lie very still. The Object and the Image in the distinct Base being reciprocal, ( as Mr. Molineux hews p.. ) of his Dioptrickj the Image there may be form - ed larger than the Object, on which depends the Doctrine of the Double Microscope. Which Instrument I believe, was first contrived, at least fitted for Use and Observation by Dr. FIool, F. R. S. and a Description of it is published in his Micrographia. Since that, Mr John Marjhall, at the Archimides in Ludgate - street, hath brought it to a very good Degree of Perfection: And I take his Double Mi - cro ] cope here described, in all Refpeds, to be the most useful, handy, and ready Instrument of this kind. I have had Mellen s Glasses, and seen Levoen - hoecI ( s and Campani ' s, but I would sooner have the Double Microscope than any of them, and the Price is much easier -

Part. p.. ) he hath been the more particular, because it is not impossible but that Microscopes may ( if not done already ) at length be improved to that perfection as to discover the Particles of Bodies on which their Colours depend. For faith he, if those Inftrumetits are or can be so far im - proved, as with sufficient diskindness t represent Objects five or six hundred times bigger than at a foot distance they appear to the naked Eye, I should hope that we might be able to discover some of the greatest: of these Corpuscles; and by one which would magnifie or thousand times, perhaps they might all be discovered, but those which pro - due blackness. And if this could be attain'd to ( vi. by Glasses to discover the constituent Par - titles of Bodies ) he fears it would be the utmost improvement of this Sense of Seeing; for it seems impossible to see the most secret and noble Works of Nature voithin the Corpuscles, because of the Transparency of these Corpuscles. miliarisherpes.c: MILIARIS Herpes. See Herpes. ' MILKY - WAY, or Via Laclea, the Galaxy, is a broad white Path or Track, encompassing the whole Heavens., and extending it self in foftie Places with a double Path, but for the most part with a single one. Some of the Ancients, as Ari - stote, cc. imagine ’ d that this Path consisted only of a certain Exhalation hanging in the Air but by the Telefcopical Oblcrvations of this Age, it hath been discovered to consist of an innumerable Quantity of Fixed Stars, different in Situation and Magnitude; from the confused Mixture of whole Light, its white Colour is supposed to be occ - signed. It passes through the Constellations of CaJJiopeia, Cygnus, Aquilla, Perfeus, Andromeda, Parc of Ophiucus, and Gemini, in the Northern Hemi - sphere and in the Southern, it takes in Part of Scorpio, Sagittarius, Centaurus, the Argo Navis, and the Ara. Metrodorus, and some Pythagoreans, thought the Sun had once gone in this Track, instead of the Ecliptick ‘ and consequently that its Whiteness proceeds from the Remains of his Light. As the Galaxy is composed of an Infinity of small Stars, so it hath usually been the Region in which new Stars have appeared: As the new Star in Cajjio - pia, which was first seen A. D. a that in - the Breast of the Swan, and another in the Knee of Serpentarius j and several others, which have ap - peared for a while, and then become invisible again.

militaryexecution.c: MILITARY Execution, is delivering a Coun - try up to be ravaged and destroyed by the Solid - ers, when it refuses to pay Contribution, &c.

mineinfortification.c: MINE, in Fortification, is a Hole dtfg or made by a Pioneer under the Rampart, or under the Face of the Bastion, whereto there are several ob - pique and winding Passages: When it is finished, divers Barrels of Powder are placed therein, to - gether with a Train or Saucidge; and the Quan - tity of Powder is proportion ’ d to the Height and Weight of the Body which is to be blown up. There are also Mines sprung in the Field, which are called Fougades. The Ally or Passage of a Mine is usually about Four Foot square, at the end of which is the Chamber of the Mine, as they call it. The far - ther it is carried on, the more it is fubjedfc to be discovered by the Enemy; therefore tis belt not to aim at Mining too far, and to make a new one where the former takes no effedl.

mine.c: MINE - D /, is a Box and Needle, with a Brass Ring divided into Degrees, with several Dyals graduated thereon; generally thus made for the Use of Miners.

minerals.c: MINERALS, are hard Bodies dug out of the Earth or Mines, ( ' whence the Name ) being in part of a Metalline, and in part of a Stony Substance, and sometimes with some Salt and Sulphur inter - mixed with the other. Of these fee a large Ac - count under the more general Word Fcfiils. See also Stones and Minerals.

minimaterminmuficl.c: MINIM, a Term in Muficl - fee Notes and Time.

minimanaturalia.c: MINIMA Naturalia, are such Particles of Mat - ter, which, tho ’ they have each a determinate Shape and Bulk, yet are too minute to be singly sensible. These are supposed to be entire, and undivided, and to be perfectly solid; and are the fame with what in another Word are called A - toms, because of their supposed Indivisibility.

muniments.c: MUNIMENTS, or rather Muniments, in Law, are the Evidences or Writings, whereby a Man is enabled to defend the Title of his Estate. And some fay this Word Miniments includes all man - ner of Evidences.
MUNIMENTS, among the Lawyers, are ta - ken for such Authentick Deeds and Writings, as a Man can defend the Title to his Land or E - state by.

minium.c: MINIUM, or ' Red - lead, is the common Calx bf Lead calcined for or Hours in a Reverbe - oratory Furnace, till it turn to a Red Colour.

minoraterminlaw.c: MINOR, a Term in Law, signifying one in Nonage, Minority, or under Age: But more pro - perly an Heir Male or Female, before they come to the Age of One and twenty during which Minority their Addons are invalid, &c. - Yet a Minor may present, as Patron to an Eccleliaftical Benefice.

minute.c: MINUTE, is the th Part of a Degree or Hour so that every Hour, or Degree of any great Circle, Is divided into Minutes, every Minute into Seconds, each Second, into Thirds, &c.

misadventureormifaventure.c: MISADVENTURE, or Mifaventure, in Law, has a special Signification, for the killing of a Man, partly by Negligence, and partly by Chance. ‘ As if a Man, thinking no Harm, carelessly throws a Stone, or fhooteth an Arrow, &c. wherewith he killeth another: In this Case he commits not Fe - long, but only lofeth his Goods, and hath Pardon of Course for his Life. Some, between Aventure and Mifaventure make this Diftindion, That A - venture is meer Chance: As if a Man, being up - on or near the W ater, he taken with some iud - den Sickness, and so fall in, and is drown ’ d or into the Fire, and be burn ’ d to Death, Mifaven - ture, they fay, is where a Man cometh to his Death by some untoward Violence as the Fall of a Tree, the Running of a Cart - wheel, the Stroke ofa Horse, or the like.

miseinlaw.c: MISE, in Law, hath several Significations: As first, a Gift or Customary Present which the Peo - ple of Wales give to every new King or Prince at their Entrance into that Principality. - Sometimes Mfes are taken for Taxes or Tollages, Anno. E. i.. Sometimes for Costs and Expences as pro Mifis ( Cuftagiis, for Costs and Charges or - dinarily used in the Entries of Judgment in Person - nal Actions. Mfe is also a Term of Art, appropriated to a Writ of Right so called, because both Parties have put themselves upon the meer Right, to be tried by the Grand AJfife, or by Battel. So that which in all other Adions is called an Issue, in a Writ of Right is called a Mise Unless a Collar teral Point be tried, and there it is called an Issue. To join the Mise upon the Meer, signifies, to join the Mise upon the Clear Right which is to join upon this I ’ oint, Whether hath more Right, the T enant or Demandant ?

misereremei.c: MISERERE Mei, or Chordapsus, is a most ve - cement Pain in the Guts, proceeding from an In - flammation of them, or Involution, and the Peri - ftaltick Motion inverted whence the Excrements are discharged by the Mouth. It is called also Volvulus.

misericordiainlaw.c: MISERICORDIA in Law, is used for an Ar - bitrary Amerciament imposed on any for an Of - fence j for where the Plaintiff or Defendant in a - ny Adion is amerced, the Entry is Sdeo in Mise. I ricordia. It is called Mifericordia, because it ought to be very moderate, and rather less than the Offence. Therefore if a Man be unreasonably a - merc ’ d in a Court, not of Record, as in the Court - Baron, &c. there is a Writ called Moderate Mifericordia, directed to the Lord or his Baliff, com - minding them that they take moderate Amercia - ments, Sometimes Mifericordia is to be quit and discharged of all manner of Amerciaments ? that a Man may fall into in the Sor'eft.

misprisonaterminlaw.c: MISPRISON, a Term in Law, signifying Neg led or Oversight. As for Example:. Mifprifion of Treason or Felony, is a Negled or Light account shewed of Treason or Felony com - mitted, by not revealing it when we know it to be committed or by letting any Person commit - ted for Treason or Felony, or Suspicion of either, to go, before he belndided. Mifprifion of Trea - fon, is the Concealment, or not disclosing of known Treason: For which, the Offenders are to liiffer Imprisonment during the King ’ s Pleasure lose their Goods, and the Profits of their Lands, during their Lives. Mifprifion of Felony, is only Finable by the Justices before whom the Party is attainted: But Justices of the Common - Pleas have Power to assess Fines and Amerciaments upon Per - sons offending by Mifprifions, Contempts, or Neg - leds, for not doing, or misdoing any thing in or concerning Fines. Mifprifion of Clerks, is a Neg - led of Clerks in writing, or keeping Records. By the Mifprifion cf Clerks, no Process ( hall be annul - led or discontinued: And JuJHces of A fife shall amend the Defaults of Clerks mifprifing of a Syl - table, or Letter, in writing.

missen.c: MISSEN - JA ? / ? of a Ship is a r & und and long piece of Timber, Standing in her Stern or stern - most Part. Some great Ships require two then that next theMain - mast, is th e Main - mijfen - and that next the Poop, the Bonaventure - missen. But when at Sea, they use the Word Mijfen alone, they always mean the Sail, and not the Mast. And to the Sail these several Terms of Art sol - lowing belong Set the Mijfen i. e. Set the Mis fen - fail right, as file ought to Hand. Change the Mijfen i. e. Bring the Mijfen - yard over to the other side of the Mast - Peek the Mijfen i. e. Put the Mijfen - yard right up and down the Mast. Spell the Mijfen, i. c. Let go the Sheet and Withal, Peek up the Tard. The Use of this Mijfen is to keep a Ship dole to a Wind: Wherefore if a Ship, be apt to Gripe too much ( as they call it ) they use no Mijfen. A Mijfen is made use of of - ten when a Ship rides at Anchor, to back her a - Stern, so that she may not foul her Anchor on the turning of the Tide. Sometimes alio they Lie a - Try, with their Mijfen only. The Length of the Mijfen is the fame with the Height of the Main - top - mast from the Quarter - deck, and the Missen - top - mast half that.

mitella.c: MITELLA, is the Surgeons Term for the Swath that holds up the Arm when it is hurt or wounded.

mittendo.c: MITTENDO manvfcriptum pediis finis, is z Writ Judicial, directed to the Treasurer and Cham - berlin of the Exchequer to search and transmit the Foot of a Fine, acknowledged before JuJHces in Eyre, into the Common - Pleas, & C.

mittimus.c: MITTIMUS, is a Writ by which Records are transferred from one Court to another, sometimes tnteedkteiy - O D immediately: As, out of the Kjng s - Bench into the Exchequer; and sometimes by a Certiorari, into the Chancery and from thence, by a Mitti - mus, into another Court. This Word is also li - ed for the Precept that is directed by a Justice of Peace to a Goaler, for the receiving and safe - keeping a Felon, or other Offender by him com - mitted to the Goal. M TRALES, are two Valves at the Orifice of the Vena pulmonaris, in the Left Ventricle of the Heart; and are so called, because, when they are joined together, they - something resemble a Mytre: They are broader than the other Valves; they are situated so as to look inwards, and do very little differ in Bigness and Form from the Fricu - sides in the right Ventricle. Their Use is to hin - der the Reflux of the Blood brought into the Left Ventricle of: the Heart by the Vena fulmonaris, back towards the Lungs again. b M VA, in Pharmacy, is the Flesh or Pulp of a Quince boiled up with Sugar into a thick Con - fiftence.

mixt.c: MIXT, i. e. a Mixt Body: By which in Chy - misty and Natural Philosophy, is understood a Body not mixt or compounded by Art, but by Na - ture; such as Minerals, Vegetables and Animals, from whom by Chymistry different Substances can be separated.
MIXT A, was anciently a Saxon Measure con - gaining Bufhels:

moatinfortification.c: MOAT, in Fortification, is a hollow Space or Ditch dug round a Town or Fortrels which is to be defended; whereof the Length and Breadth often depends upon the Nature of the Soil, ac - cording as it is Marshy or Rocky. But Moats in general may be from to Fathom broad, and from to Foot deep.. Dry Moat, is that which is destitute of Water, and ought to be deeper than one that is full of Water. Lined Moat, is that whole Scarp and Counter - scarp are cas ’ d with a Wall of Mafons Work lying In Talus or a - soap. ' Flat - bottom d Moat, is that which hath no Heap - ing, its Corners being somewhat rounded. AH Moats must be well flanked, and in general so wide, as that no Ladder, Tree, &c. can reach a - cross it. If the Ditch be dry, or has but little Water, there is usually another small Trench cut quite along the middle of it.

moderatemifericordia.c: MODERATE Mifericordia, is a Writ for him that is amerced in a Court Baron, or other being not of Record, for any Tranfgrelfion or Offence beyond the Quality of a Fault. It is dire & ed to the Lord of the Court, or his Bayliff, command - ing them to take a moderate Amerciament of the Party, and is founded upon Magna Chart a, cap.. Quod nullus liber homo amercietur nififecundum qua - Utatem delicti, &c.

modillonsormodillions.c: MODILLONS, or Modillions, in Architecture, are little Brackets which are often fet under the Cornices, more especially in the Corinthian and Ccmpofit Order, and serve to support the Prove - cure of the Larmier or Drip. The Word comes from the Italian Modiglion, signifying a little Mo - del or Measure; but this Part must be distinguish - ed from the great Model, which is the Diameter of the Pillar: For as the Proportion of an Edifice in general depends on the Diameter of the Pillar; so the Size and Number of the Modi lions, as also the Interval between them ought to have due Re - lation to the whole Fabrick.

modiolus.c: MODIOLUS, T repanum, or Anabaptijlon, is an ' Instrument which they use in profound Corrupt tions, Contufions, Cuts, and Fractures of the Bones of the Head, not to be applied; unless,. The Chips and Prominences of the Bones prick.. When the Upper Table is entire, but depress ’ d; and the Lower broken.. When the extra aba - ted Blood would choak a Man with Corruption. The manner of Trepanning, or opening the Skull is thus: When the Hairs are ( haven off, the Skin is to be cut to the Pericranium, avoiding, as care - fully as may be, the Muscles of the Temples, and the Sutures of the Skull; and for this time the Wound is to be bound up, unless there be so little Blood spilt, that the Membrane, called Pericrani - um, may at the fame time be pulled off from the Skull. Then after a few Hours you may stop the Ears of the Patient, take one of these Instru - ments, called a Masculine Modiolus, whose Point is to be fixed in the SkuU, but so far off the Fra - cure, that it touch it not, much less the Suture, with its Teeth; tho ’ some Surgeons never avoid the Sutures, and assure us that they have persona - ted them as successfully as any other Part: Then hold the Instrument fast with the Left Hand, and turn it round with the Right, ’ till you have cut a pretty deep Hole: After this take a Feminine Modiolus, ( which has no Point in the middle ) and turn it round, as before. In the mean time take away the Dust or Chips that proceed ! from the Perforation, and moisten the Instrument in Oyl and Water, to make it cool and slippery. The Blood that appears, will ( hew that you are now gone as deep as thefecond Table, i. e. beyond the Skull, to the Meninx and then you must press very gently, left the Membrane of the Brain be unadvisedly hurt. When the Bone begins to wag, put ( something in betwixt the sides of the Wound; loosen it, and take it out with a pair of Surgeon ’ s Pincers. Blanchard.

mood.c: MOOD & Forma, are Words of Art in Pro - cess and Pleadings; and namely, in the Answer of the Defendant; whereby he denieth himself to have done the Thing laid to his Charge, Mo - do & forma declarata It signifies as much as that Clause in the Civil Law, legat allegata prout allegantur, case vera where mo do & forma are of the Substance of thelffue, and were but Words of course.

moduleormodel.c: MODULE, or Model, in Architecture, is a certain Measure invented by Vignola, and made use of to regulate the Proportion of the whole Building. It is generally half the Diameter of a Pillar at the lower end, in the Tuscan and in the Doricli Order; but in others, the whole Diame - ter. This Diameter is divided into equal Parts; and into for the Ionich, Corinthian, and Compofit Orders. And this Module or Model is a kind of Universal Measure, which helps us, ‘ ' ' " to M O to get rid of the great Uncertainties there are in the Feet and Inches of divers Nations, and at di - vers Times.

modusdecimmdi.c: MODUS Decimmdi, is when either Land, a Sum of Money, or Yearly Pension, is given to the Parson, ( c. by Composition, as Satisfaction for his Tythesin kind.

moineau.c: MOINEAU, is a Name the French, andlome Modern Writers of Fortification, give to a little Plat - Bastion, which is raised before a Curtain that is too long, and Which hath two other Bastions at the ends of it for they being out of Musket - shot one of the other, must be defended by some such hing as this Moineau or Plat - Bastion. Some - times the Moineau joins to the Curtain, and some - times is disjoined from it by a Moat.

moltgenu.c: MOLT Genu, Patella or Rotula, is a round and broad Bone, placed at the jointing of the Thigh and Leg, to preserve the Knee from flip - king out, and to defend the Juncture from Enter - nal Injuries.

moltcame.c: MOLT Came a, is a Fleshy and sometimes a Sp'opgy Substance, without Bones or Bowels: It is often black, like concreted Blood and some - times extreat hard; preternaturally brought into to the World instead of a Foetus.

moline.c: MOLINE. The Heralds Term for one of their Cfoffes of this Figure. Tire Field Assure, Cross Moline Or, by the Name ofMo / ineux. Guillim faith this Cross reprefenteth a Mill - Rind, or tile Form of the Ink of a Mill.

molossus.c: MOLOSSUS, is the Foot of a Latin Verse, consisting of Three Syllables, when they are all long.

moments.c: MOMENTS, are sometimes taken for the least and most insensible Parts of Time; as when we fay, such a thing was done in a Mo - ment. In Mathematicks, Moments are such indeter - ’ minare and instable Parts of Quantity, as are supposed to be in perpetual flux, i. e. either continually decreasing or increasing; which latter are taken for Affirmative and Positive Moments, and the former for Negative of SubtraCtible ones And these continually increasing or decreasing Particles are supposed to be infinitely small; for as soon as ever they come to be of any finite Mag - nitude, they cease to be Moments. Moments there - fore are to be look ’ d upon as the generative Prin - ciples of finite Magnitudes and are here suppo - fed to have no Magnitude, but to be Inceptive on - ly of it, to use Dr. Wallis his Word. And because ’ tis the fame thing, if in the room of these Moments, the Velocities of their In - creafes or Decreases be made use of, or the finite Quantities proportionable to such Velocities this ' Method of proceeding, which considers the Mo - rions, Changings, or Fluxions of Quantities, hath come to be called Fluxions. Moments also in a Physical Sense, as they are used in reference to the Laws of Motion, signifie the Quantities of Motion in any moving Bodies and sometimes, simply, the Motion it self; and they define it to be the Vis in fit a, or Potter by which any moving Bodies do continually change their Places. And in comparing the Motions of Bodies, the P atioof theie Moments is always compounded of the Quantity of Matter in, and the Celerity of the moving Body: So that the Moment of any moving ' Body may be considered as a Rett angle under the Quantity of Matter into the Celerity. And since ’ tis certain that all equal Rectangles have their Sides reciprocally proportionable, (. . Eucl. ) therefore if the Moments of any Mo - veables are equal, the Quantity of Matter in one, to that of the other, will be reciprocally:: as the Celerity of the Latter to the Celerity of the For - mer: And vice versa, if the Quantities of Mat - ter are reciprocally proportionable to the Celeri - ties, the Moments or Quantities of Motion in each will be equal. The Moment of any moving Body may be con - fidered also as the Aggregate or Sum of all the Moments of the Parts of that Body and there - fore. where the Magnitudes and Number of any Particles are the fame, and where they are mo - ved with the fame Celerity, there will be the fame Moments of the Wholes.

monochord.c: MONOCHORD, a kind of Instrument anci - ently of singular Use for the Regulating of Sounds but some appropriate the Name of Monochord to an Instrument that hath only one Angle String, as the - Trumpet Marine, The Ancients made use of the Monochord to determine the Proportion of Sounds to one ano - ther: When the Chord Was divided into two e - qual Parts, so that the Terms were as and, they called them Unifons but if they Were as. to, they called them Oclaves or Diapafns when they were as to, they called them Fifths, of Diapentes if they were as to, they called them Fourths, or Diatejferons if the Terms were as to, they call it Diton, or a T rce major but if the Terms were as to, then they called it a Detni - diton, or a Tierce minor - and lastly, if the Terms were as to, they called it a Demiton or Die e. The Monochord being thus divided, was pro - perly that Which they called a Syfem, of which there were many kinds, according to the different Divisions of the Monochord.
MONOCHORD. See the accurate Division of the Monochord in Phil. Trans. N.. by Dr Wallis.

monopetalousflowers.c: MONOPETALOUS Flowers, fin Botany ) are such, as, tho ’ they may be seemingly cut into four or five ' small Petala or Leaves, are yet all of one piece, and which falling off all together, have their Flower in one piece. See Petala.

monopolyinlaw.c: MONOPOLY, in Law, is a Grant to any Per fon or Persons, of or for the some buying, felling, - making, working, or using any Commodity,

monotriglyphaterminarchitecture.c: MONOTRIGLYPH, a Term in Architecture, signifying the Space of one Triglyph between two Pi Infers, or two Columns.

monstrans.c: MONSTRANS De droit, in a Legal Sense, figiiifies a Suit in Chancery, fof the SubjeCt to be restored to Lands and Tenements, which he ( hews to be his Right, tho ’ by Office found to be in the j Polfefion of another lately dead by which Office j the King is entitled to a Chattel, Free - hold, of Inheritance in the laid Lands, I

MONSTRANS De faits ou Records, Jheveing of Deeds or Records,, is thus: Upon an Adlion of Debt brought upon an Obligation, after the Plaintiff hath declared, he ought to shew his Obligation; and so it is of Records. And the Difference be - tween Monfir ans de fnits and Or de faits, is this: He that pleads the Deed or Records, or declares upon it, ought to shew the fame; and the other, against whom such Deed or Record is pleaded, may demand Oyer of the fame.

monstraverunt.c: MONSTRAVERUNT, is a Writ that lies for the Tenants in Ancient Demesne, being distrained for the Payment of any Toll or Imposition, con - trary to their Liberty which - they do or should enjoy.

montpagnote.c: MONT Pagnote, or the Pofi of the Invulnerable, is an Eminence chosen out of Cannon - shot of a Place besieged; where curious and wary Persons place themselves to see the Attack and the manner of the Siege.

month.c: MONTH, properly speaking, is the Time in. which the Moon runs through the Zodiack, and therefore is accounted by the Motion of the Moon; and therefore the Lunar Month is either Period - cal, which is the Time of the Moon ’ s Motion from any one Point of the Zodiack to the fame again, and is something less than Days and Hours; or else Synodical, which is the Time between New Moon and New Moon, and is something more than, Days and an half. There is also a Solar Month, which is the Time that the Sun takes up in running through one of the Signs of the Zodiack, and is almost Days and half. And both these Solar and Lunar Months are either Astronomical, like thole above mentioned; or Civil, which are various, according to the U - sage of accounting in different Places, Cities and Nations. The Egyptians accounted by Solar Months, each of Days; and to compleat their Year, after such Months, they added Days, which the odd Hours made up. But most of the Ancient Nations accounted by the Lunar Synodical Month as the Jews, Greeks, and the Romans, ’ till J. Cafiars Time; and as the Mahometans do to this Day. And because these Months did not contain an exact Number of Days, to adapt them to Civil Computation, they accounted alternately one Month to have, and the next Days; and by this means they made two such Civil Months to be equal to two Lunar ones of Days and half; and they brought it to pass, that the New Month, fora Run of many Years, did not much deviate from the First Day of the Civil Month.

moodsingrammar.c: MOODS in Grammar, determine the Signifi - cation of Verbs, as to the Manner and Circum - stances of the Affirmation; and are in Number Six, vi. The Indicative, the Imperative, the Op - native, the Subjunctive, and the Infinitive Mood; which fee.

moodinmusick.c: MOOD in Musick., signifies certain Proportions of the Lime, or Measure of Notes. These Moods or Modes of measuring Notes, were formerly Four in Number, vi. . The PerfeB of the More, in which a Large contain ’ d three Longs, a Long three Breves, a Breve three Semi - breves, and a Semi - brev ? three Minims. . The P erf eel of the Less, wherein a Large comprehended two Longs, a Long two Breves, a Breve three Semi - breves, and a Semi - breve two Minims. . The Imperfect of the. More, in which a Large contained two Longs, a Long two Breves, a Breve two Semi - breves, and a Semi - breve three Minims. . The Imp erf eB of the Less, i the fame with that which we call the Common Mood, the other three being now altogether out of Use; altho the Measure of our Common Triple - time is the fame with the Blood, ImperfcEl of the Blorc, except that we reckon but two Minims to a Semi - breve, which in that Mood comprehend three. In our Common Mood, two Longs make one Large, two Breves a Long, two Semi - breves a Breve, cc. proceeding in the fame Order to the last or shortest Note; So that a Large contains two Longs, four Breves, eight Semi - breves, fix - teen Minims, thirty two Crotchets, sixty four Qua - vers, cc. Besides these Moods of Time, Five others real - ting to Tune, were in Use among the Ancient Grecians, which were termed Tones or Tunes by the Latins the Design of either being to ( hew in what Key a Song was fet, and how the different Keys had relation one to another. These forts of Moods were dish'nguifh ’ d by the Names of the several Provinces of Greece, where they were first invented; as the Dor if, Lydian, Ionicl, Phrygian, and SEolick, Doricfi Mood consisted of flow - tun ’ d Notes, and was proper for the exciting Persons to Sobrie - ty and Piety. Lydian Mood was likewise used in Solemn Grave Musick; and the Descant or Composition was of flow Time, adapted to Sacred Hymns or Anthems. Ionick, Mood was for more light and soft Mu - sick; such as pleasant amorous Songs, Sarabands, Corants, Jiggs, &c. Phrygian Mood was a Warlike kind of Mu - sick, fit for Trumpets, Hautboys, and other Instruments of the like Nature; whereby the Minds of Men were animated to undertake Military At - chievements, or Martial Exercises. dEolick. Mood, being of a more airy, soft, and delightful Sound, such as our Madrigals, served to allay the Palflons by the means of its grateful Variety and melodious Harmony. hese Moods or Tones were distinguished into Authentic and P loyal, with respect to the divi - ding of the OElave into its Fifth and Fourth: The Former was when the Fifth Poflefled the Lower Place, according to the Harmonica ! Divifi - on of an O Slave and the other was when it flood in the Upper Place, according to the Arithmeti - cal Division of the fame Octave, ) MOON. MOO MOO

moon.c: MOON. The Periodical Revolution of the Moon, in reference to the Fixed Stars, is Days, Hours, Minutes: And in the fame Space of Time, by a strange Correspondence and Har - many of the two Motions, it revolves the fame way about its own Axis; whereby ( one Motion as much converging it to, as the other turns it from the Earth ) the fame side is always exposed to our Sight. See Vol... The Librations of the Moon ’ s Body which oc - casion that the fame Hemisphere exactly is not always exposed to our Sight, arise from the Ec - centricity of the Moon ’ s Orbit, from the Pertur - bations by the Sun ’ s Attraction, and from the Obliquity of the Axis of the Diurnal Rotation of the Moon ’ s own Orbit; without the Knowledge of which Circumstances, her Phenomena were in - explicable, but by the Consideration of them arc very demonstrable. The Mean Horary Motion of the Moon, in rested: of the Fix ’ d Stars, is Minutes, Se - conds, Thirds, Fourths and an half. The Moon is distant from the Earth, accord - ing to molt Astronomers,; according to Vin - deline,; Copernicus,; Kfrcher, - f; and according to Tycho, - f Semi - diameters of the Earth. Sir If. Newton thinks the Distance ought to be esteemed about: Therefore the Mean Distance may be reckoned. But if the Earth and Moon move both round the Sun, with their Common Centre of Gravity, that Admirable A - astronomer demonstrates that the Distance between the Centres of the Earth and Moon will be y of the Earth ’ s Semi - diameter, Prop. o. Lib.. Princip. She is nearer the Earth at her Sygygy, than in the Quadrature, by Part of the Distance. According to M. Cajfmi, the Moon ’ s greatest Distance from the Earth is r, the mean Distance, and the least Distance Semi - diameters of. the Earth. The Power of the Moon ’ s Influence, as to the Tides, is to that of the Sun as to one. Sir If. Newton. As to the Inequality of the Mooffs Motion, ( which proceeds from the Action of the Sun, di - fturbing the Motion of the Secondary Planets ) she moves swifter, and describes ( by a Radius drawn from it to the Earth ) a greater Area in proportion to the Time, hath an Orbit less cur - ved, and by that means comes nearer to the Earth in her Sy ygies or Conjunctions, than in the Qua - dratures, unless the Motion of her Eccentricity hinder it: Which Eccentricity is greatest, when the Apogeum of the Moon happens in the Con - junctions; and is least, when the - Apogeum hap - pens at the Quadratures. And therefore the Moon is swifter as well as nearer to us in her Perigeum, and more remote and flower in her Apogeum at the Conjunctions, than at the Quadratures; and her Motion is swifter also in the Earth ’ s Aphelion, than in its Perihelion. The Apogeum also goes forward swifter in the Conjunctions, and goes flower at the Quadratures: But her Nodes are at reft in the Conjunctions, and do recede molt swift - ly in the Quadratures. The Moon also perpetually changes the Figure of her Orbit, or the Species of the Ellipse she moves in. There are also some other Inequalities in the Motions of this Planet, which can hardly be re - duced to any certain Rule: As, that the Veloci - ties or ' Horary Motions of the Apogeum and Nodes, and their Equations, and the Difference between the greatest Eccentricity in the Conjun - ctions, and the least in the Quadratures; and that Inequality which is called the Variation of the Moon: All these do encrease and decrease annu - ally, in a Triplicate Ratio of the apparent Dia - meter of the Sun: And this Variation is encreased and diminished in a Duplicate Ratio of the Time between the Quadratures; as Sir If. Newton proves in many places of his Principia. That Curious Person found the Apogeum in the Moon ’ s Sygygies to go forward min. each Day, in respect of the Fix ’ d Stars; and tp go backward min. j each Day in the Quadratures: And therefore the middle Annual Motions he estimates at deg. This differs something from Mr. FI am seed's A - astronomical Tables; where the Diurnal Prog res - sion of the Moon ’ s Apogeum is min. fe - conds in th e Sy ygies, and the Recession min. seconds in the Quadratures. See the Words Secondary Planets. That the Cause of the Secondary Light of the Moon, as they call it; that is, theoblcure Part of her, appearing like kindled Allies, just before and after the Change or New Moon, is the Sun ’ s Rays reflected from the bright Hemisphere of the Earth to thole dark Parts of the Moon, and thence again jrefle & ed to the Earth destitute of the Sun ’ s Light; fee proved in fucchiw Philofopb Optic. Nov. from p. to p.. And also in Tacpuets Opera Geometrica. The Excellent Sir If. Newton makes it a Prop - sition to enquire into the Figure of the Moon; and supposing it, at its first Original, to have been a Fluid, like to our Sea, he calculates that ' the Attraction of our Earth would raite the Wa - ter there to near Foot high, as the Attraction of the Moon ariseth our Water to Foot; Whence the Figure of the Moon must be a She - rhoid, whole greatest Diameter extended, will pass through the Centre of our Earth; and will be longer than the other Diameter perpendicular to it, by Feet. And from hence it comes to pass that we fee always the fame Face of the Moon: For slie Cannot reft in any other Position, but will continually endeavour to conform her self to this Situation. Prop.. Lib.. The Moon hath properly no Atmosphere, such as our Earth hath, abounding with Clouds, Winds, Thunder, or Lightning; because her Face al - ways ( when our Air is clear ) appears distend: and clear; and by our Telescopes we can see the Sun ’ s Light pass regularly and uniformly from one Mountainous Place to another. Mr. Flamfeed in Philofopb. Trarf N. mooratsea.c: MOOR at Sea, signifies the laying out the An - chors of a Ship so, as is best and fafeft for her ’ Riding. There are several ways of Mooring a Ship. Sometimes they Moor her a Thwart, by laying one Anchor on one side of a River, and a - nother right against it on the other side; in order to make both the Cables bear together, as, well at Tide of Ebb, as at Flood. To Moor Alongst, is to lay one Anchor right m the middle of the Stream, and another right a head of the Ship, which is done when they are in danger of driving shoar; for by this means both her Anchors do bear together, and so will save her from falling on either Shore. To Moor iVater - Jhot, is to Moor a Ship in the middle between the two former ways, quarter - ing as it were, neither across the Tide, nor a - longest it, but between both. When a Ship comes into a Place of Riding, the Master and his Mates observe on what Point of the Compass the Wind is likelieft to endanger the Ship, and there they lay out an Anchor; and this is called Mooring for East, North, See. according to the Point file is Moored upon. They don ’ t fay a Ship is Moor - ed, unless she have at lead two Anchor ’ s out j except in one Case, and that is, when, tho ’ ihe V have but one Anchor out, yet there is a Hawser afhoarj and then they fay fire is Moored with her Head to the ShoatP MOORSHEAD, is the Head of a Copper, or Glass - Still, or Alembick, which is luted on to the ' Body, or Cucurbit; and hath a Beak, Nose, or Pipe, to let the raised Spirit run down into the Receiver.

mortgageinlaw.c: MORTGAGE, in Law, signifies a Pawn of Land, or Tenements, or any thing moveable, laid or bound for Money borrowed, to be the Cre - ditors for ever, if the Money be not paid at the Day agreed upon: And the Creditor holding Land, or Tenement upon this Bargain, is called Tenant in Mortgage. mothertongues.c: MOTHER Tongues, in Latin, Matrices Lin - gua, are such Languages as seem to have no De - tendance upon. But now the Languages cased in the World, do far exceed that Number: - If you will believe Pliny and Strabo, there was a Town in Colchos called Dio four i a, to which Men ' of three hundred Nations, and as many several Languages, did Resort for Trading. Language or Mother - Tongue by them - selves. And Purchas tells us, Pilgr. Lib.. Sed.. Cap. i. That by Converse and Enquiry, in the Northern Parts of America, about Florida, he found more than different Languages amongst the Inhabitants of those Places. Joseph Scaliger affirms there are no more than Eleven Mother - Tongues used in Europe of which Four are of more, general and large Ex - ' tent, and the other Seven of a narrower Com - pass and Use. . The Greek, which was anciently of very great Extent, not only in Europe, but in Ajia and Africk too, where several Colonies of that Nation were planted; by which Dispersion and Mixture with other People, it did degenerate into several DialeEls. Besides those Four that are commonly noted, the Doric, Ionic, Molic, Attic, Herodotus doth mention Four several Dialeds of the Ionic. The Inhabitants of Bjoodes, Cyprus, Crete had each of them some Peculiarity in their Language: if; ' r ’: ' - f ' ' ‘ Y ' And the present Coptic or Egyptian seems, both from the Words, and the Character, to be a Branch of this Family, and was probably spread amongst that People in the Days of Alexander the Great, upon his conquering of them, thos some conceive that there were at Ieaft Families of Greeks planted in that Country long before his Time. . The Latin, tho this be much of it a Deri - vation from the Greek, ( of which the now French, Spanijh, and Italian, are several Off - springs and Derivations ) had anciently Four several Dialeds, as Petrus Crinitus strews out of Harr, . The Sclavonic is extended, tho ’ with some Va - ration, through many large Territories, Mufcovia, Poland, Bohemia, Vandalia, Croatia, Lithuania, Dalmatia and is said to be the Vulgar Language used amongst Sixty several Nations. motion.c: MOTION, is a continual and successive Mu - tation or Change of Place. All Motion may be consider'd either Absolutely or Relatively. Also - lute Motion is the Change of the Locus Absolutus of any moving Body, and therefore its Celerity will be measured by the Quantity of the Also - lute Space which the Moveable hath run through. But Relative Motion is a Mutation of the Real - tive or Vulgar Place of the moving Body, and so hath its Celerity accounted or measured by the Quantity of Relative Space which the Move - able runs over. All Motion is of it self redilinear, or made according to strait Lines, with the fame conflant uniform Velocity, if no external Cause make any Alteration in its Direction. If a Body, moving uniformly, and with the fame Degree of Velocity, pass over two Spaces, the Times of the Motions will be as the Spaces as is very plain to him that will confider it. If a Body move through two ' Spaces in equal Times, thole Spaces will be to one another as the Velocities of the Motions. If two Bodies move uniformly, but with un - equal Velocities, through the fame Space, the Times will be as the Velocities. If two Bodies, moving uniformly, go with un - equal Velocities, the Spaces which will be past over by them in unequal Times, will be to one another in a Ratio compounded of that of the Velocities and that of the Times. Galileus, de Motu Local. Dial.. Giorn. terra. If any Bodies are impelled upwards by dise - rent Forces, they will be railed to different Heights; which Heights will be to one another as the Squares of their Velocities. And if Bodies fall from different Altitudes, the Celerities will be to one another as the Squares of such Altitudes. M O T I O N Its Lam. The Incomparable Sir Isaac Newton gives but these Three Laws of Motion, which may be truly called Laws of Nature. . That every Body will continue in its State, either of Reft, or Motion uniformly forward in a Right Line, unless it be made to change that State by some Force impressed upon it. . That the Change of Motion is proportion - able to the moving Force impressed j and is al - ways according to the Direction of that Right Line in which the Force is impressed. . That ReaRion is always equal and contrary to Adion j or, which is all one, the mutual Add - ons of two Bodies one upon another are equal, and directed towards contrary Parts: As when ne Body presses and draws another, ’ tis as much pressed or drawn by that Body. The Quantity of any Motion is discoverable by the joint Consideration of the Quantity of Matter in, and the Velocity of the moving Bo - dy: For the Motion of any Whole, is the Sum f the Motions of all the Parts. And consequent - ly if a Body be twice as great as another, and be moved with an equal Degree of Velocity, the Quantity of the Motion is double in the Former but if the Velocity be also double, their the Quantity of the Motion is Quadruple of that of the latter. Newtons Princip. The Quantity of Motion, which is found by tad king either the Sum of Motions made the fame way or the Difference of those which are made contrary ways, is not at all changed by the Action of Bodies one upon another. For Adion and Readion are always equal, ( by Law. ) wherefore ( by Law. ) they must needs produce equal Changes in the Motions towards contrary Parts: Wherefore if the Motions be both according to the fame Diredi - on, whatsoever is added to the Body to be moved or which is forced to give place, is subdued from the Body which moves, or drives away the other j lb that the Sum remains the fame as be - fore. But if the Bodies meet with contrary Di - regions, there must be an equal Subftradion of the Motion of each, and consequently the Diffe - rence of the Motions made towards the contrary parts, will remain the fame. Suppose the She - rical Body A to be thrice as big as B, and of the like Figure. Let A have two Degrees of Velocity, and B pursue it with ten Degrees of Velocity Wherefore the Quantity of the Motion of A to, is as to o; therefore the Sum of the Motions of both is. Suppose then B to overtake A, and to give it,, or Degrees of Velocity j ’ tis plain it must lose just as much it feif: Where - fore A will go on with,, Parts of Veloci - ty i and B will follow after with,, or. So that the Sum will still be and thus will it always be. Idem. Mr. Keil, in his LcSliones Physica, proves this diftindly, by branching of it into two Theorems. See A -,. Which THEOREMS are these. I. MOTION: From the first of Sir If. Newtons three Laws of Motion or Nature mentioned under this word Motion in. Vol. I. by way of Corollary may be inferred, ( i. j That no Particle of Matter, or any Combination of such ( That is, no Body whatever ) can either move of it self, or alter the direction of its Motion, because ’ tis entirely pas - five and indifferent as to motion or reft; so that neither Motion or Reft are essential to Matter. (. ) ’ Tis plain also from hence, that naturally of it self, no Body can ever move in a Curve Line; for since all Motion is originally and naturally re - ctilinear, ’ tis impossible that any Body can move in a Curve or Line that is not strait of it self; be - cause then it must of it self continually alter the di - section of its Motion which cannot be, by the for - mer Corollary; wherefore the Motion of the Hea - venly Bodies in Circles or Ellipses cannot be ac - counted for by the Natural Laws of Motion; but it is owing to the Will of the great Creator that they are kept in their Orbits, by an attractive force. From the Second of the three Laws of Motion it follows, that all Effects will always be proportional to their Adequate Causes; and thus if a - ny degree of any force will produce any degree of Motion, a double degree of the fame force vill produce a double degree of Motion, a Triple, a Triple, and so on in any Ratio whatsoever. And this Motion must proceed on in the fame Dire - dion with that of the moving Force, because ’ tis from That only that the Motion arises; and Bo - dies once in motion cannot change their direction of themselves. And if a. Body be already in motion, the moti - on arising from a force impress ’ d, if it be in the fame direction with that of the former Motion, it will encrease it in proportion to its power; but if k be impressed in a contrary Direction, it destroys the former Motion either totally or in part, that is, equal to the force of the Impreffipn. And when it hath ' a Direction any way Oblique to that of the former Motion, it is either added to, or fob - traded from it, according as a Motion arising from a Composition of those two, is determined.

mound.c: MOUND. The Term in Heraldry for a Ball or Globe, with a Cross upon ir, such as our Princes are usually drawn or painted with, hold - ing it in their Left Hand, as they do the Sceptre in their Right. Mound also signifies a Fence or Hedge.

moyenau.c: MOYENAU fa French Term ) in Fortification is a small flat Bastion, commonly placed ’ in the middle of an over - long Curtain, by which the Ba - ftions at the Extremities are not well defended from the Small - shot, by reason of their Distance; so that this Work is proper for placing in it a Bo - dy of Mufqueteers to fire upon the Enemy from all sides. After this, he gives an Account of Experiments made with the Mucilage; the mo ft of which come to this, That all Acids do coagulate it, as all Au - ftercs and Austere Acids; but with this Difference, that the Coagulum or Curd made by Acids only, is tendered than that which is produced by an Austere only, or an Austere Acid.

mucrocordis.c: MUCRO Cordis, or Apex, is the Lower point - ed end of the Heart.

mucronated.c: MUCRONATED, is whatever ends or term - nates in a Point, like that of a Sword, &c.

muffleinchymistry.c: MUFFLE in Chymistry, is the Cover of a T eft or Copper, which is put over it in the Fire.

mullettheterminheraldry.c: MULLET, the Term in Heraldry for a Star of Five Points, of this Figure j and is usually the M U C

mucilage.c: MUCILAGE fin Pharmacy ) is a viscous Ex - traction made of Seeds, Gums, Roots, &c. with Water.

mucilaginousglands.c: MUCILAGINOUS Glands, are a numerous fort ef Glands leated in the Joints, first, I think, particularly taken notice of by Dr. Havers, in his Ojleologia: He faith these are of two forts, some are final, and in a manner Miliary Glands being Glandules placed all upon the fame Surface of the Membrane, which lies over the Articulations The other fort are conglomerated, or many Glan - rules collected and planted one upon another, so as to make a Bulk, and appear conspicuously, and are considerable Glands. In some of the Joints there are several of them, in others there is a Angle Gland. For the Structure of these large Glands, they consist of small Vesicles, which are not gathered into several Lobules or Bags of Glandules, but are disposed upon several Membranes lying one over another; of which Membranes there are several in every one of these Glands, which appear vi - dently in them that are Hydropical. They have their Blood - Vessels, as other Glands, but their Veins have a particular Flexure in their Course for retarding the Return of the Blood from the Glands, that the mucilaginous Liquor, which is not separated with the greatest Expedition, may have Time to penetrate the secretary Pores of the Glandules. The Large Mucilaginous Glands are variously seated; some in a Sinus, formed in the Joint; others Hand near or over - against the Interstice between the Articulated Bones; but in general they are so placed, as to be squeeze ’ d gently, and lightly press ’ d in the Inflexion or Extension of the Joint, so as to separate a Quantity of Much - lage proportionate to the Motion of the Part, and the present Occasion, and yet without any Injury. The Design of all these Glands is to separate a mucilaginous kind of Liquor that serves princi - pally to lubricate the Joints, to make them so ship - very, as to be moved with the greatest Facility imaginable. It serves likewise to prelerye the Ends of the Articulated ' Bones from Attrition, and an immoderate Incalelcence. But all these Things it performs in Conjunction with the Ma - dullard Oil of which two Ingredients, is made a Composition, admirably fitted for these Ends: For the Mucilage adds to the Lubricity of the Oyl, and the Oyl preserves the Mucilage from growing too thick and viscous. The Doctor observes the fame fort of Glands to lie between the Muscles and Tendons, and sup - poses that there is the fame Mixture of an Oyly and Mucilaginous Substance; the one being that Fat which is found between the Muscles, and is supply ’ d by the Adipoie Glands; the other being separated by the Mucilaginous Glandules, of which the common Membrane of the Muscles is every where full. This Mixture in the Inter ftices of the Muscles lubricates them and their Tendons, and preserves them from Ihrinking, and from growing dry and rigid. For the Generation of this Mucilage, he sup - poses that Nature has designed one large Viscus, and that this is the Office of the Spleen; the Glandules of which he makes to have two fe - cretory Pores; by one of which some Acid, and by the other, some Austere Particles are separated; Difference or Distinguishing Mark for the Third ! Multiplication is only a Compendious Addition, effedfing at once what in the ordinary way of Ad - dition would require many Operations: For the Multiplicand is only added to it leis, or repeated, as often as the Unites of the Multiplicator do ex - press. Thus if were to be multiplied by, the ProduB is, which is the Sum arising from the Addition of Four times to it self. In all Multiplication, as x is to the Multiplica - tor, so is the Multiplicand to the ProduB. Whence tis plain, that in Multiplication of Integers, the ProduB must be greater than either of the FaBors, ( for so the Multiplicator and Multiplicand are called, because - between them they make up the ProduB ) because either FaBor is greater than Unity. But in Multiplication of Fractions, the ProduB mull be less in Value than either of the FaBors, because they are both less than Unity. Thus, the ProduB of, multiplied by, is greater than either or; but, the ProduB of t, multiplied by is less in Value than either or f.
