murageinlaw.c: MURAGE, in Law, signifies a Toll or Tribute to be levied for building or repairing ofPublick Walls j and is due either by Grant or Prefcripri - on. It seems also to be a Liberty granted to a Town by the King, for the collecting Money to - wards the Walling of the fame.

murder.c: MURDER, according to our Law, is a willful and felonious killing of another upon prepensed Malice, whether secretly or openly, and whether English - man or Foreigner living under the King ’ s Protection. And this prepensed Malice is Twofold:. Express, When it may be evidently proved that there was Ill - will;. Implied, When one killeth a - nother suddenly, having nothing to defend himself, as going over a Stile, - or such like: For in such a Case, or when a Man killeth a meer Stranger, the Law prefumeth that he had Malice again ft him, or else he would not do it without any man - ner of Provocation.

murderers.c: MURDERERS, are small Pieces of Ordnance, either of Brass or Iron, having Chambers ( ' that is Charges made of Brass or Iron ) put in at their Breeches: They are mostly used at Sea, at the Bulk - heads of the Fore - castle, Half - deck, or See - j ridge, in order to clear the Decks when an Ene - my boards the Ship; they are fastned and tra - veled by a Pintle, which is put into a Stock.

muscle.c: MUSCLE, the chief Instrument of Voluntary Motion in an Animal Body. The Parts of a Muf - cle are Three its Bead, Belly, and Tail. The Head of a Muscle is its Beginning, and as it were the Centre of its Motion - and this is always fix - ed to the roost stable Part. The Belly of a Muf - cle is its Middle Part, which is tumid, or extend - ed, in all Muscular Motion: The Tail is the o - ther End or Extream, which is fastned into the Part to be moved. Muscular Motion, or which way the Belly of a Muscle comes to be swelled, and consequently its Extreams brought nearer together, in order to move the Part required, is a very great Mystery as indeed many other Things are in an Human Body, which is fearfully and wonderfully made There have been many Hypotheses to solve this which, whether fatisfaeftory or not, must be left to every ones Judgment to determine. Dr. Willis supposes the Animal Spirits, brought by the Nerves, to be lodged in the Tendons of the Muscles, and that meeting with other Acflive Par - titles brought from the Blood, they make an Ef - fervcfccnce j by which the carnous Fibres of the Muscle are agitated, fluffed, and swelled, and so the whole Muscle is contracted in its Length. Stem imagines the carnous Fibres of the Muscles ' as alio the opposite Tendons, to be in their Con - ftru &: ure like to Parallelograms - by an Alteration of the Angles of which, the Muscle is contracted, and the Head and ail brought near together And this he thinks may be done without the Ac - cession of any New Matter. Dr. May falls nearly in with Dn Willis his Notion: He thinks the Contraction of the Must cle is made by an Effervescence, arising from the Mixture of the Sulphurous Saline Particles of the Blood, with the Bitro - aerious ones brought by the Nerves, which blow up and distend the Belly of the Muscle. M. Du Verne ) fancies this Infumefcence may be made without Fermentation, by the Animal Spirits and a Juice from the Arteries, running into the ' Tendons and carnous Fibres, and so extending themselves, as Ropes and Cats - gut - strings swell in moist " Weather. Dr. Crown supposes every carnous Fibre to be made up of small Globules or Bladders, all opening one into another, into which the nutritious Juice, and one or two other fine and restive Liquors en - thing, do, by means of the natural Heat, make an Ebullition or Effervescence by which means the whole Body of the Muscle becomes extended, and its Length contracted, &c. Boreili takes the Fibres of a Muscle to consist of a Chain of divers Bfombs or Lozenges, whose Areas are capable of being enlarged or contracted, according as the nervous Juice, together with the Lymph a and Blood, are let and forced into or out of them, ad Imperium Amm, e, The Accurate Mr. Cowper seems to think the Blood to be the true Pondus, by which the AElion of a Muscle is composed: and that either by Turgescence begun in the Parietes of the Cells of the Fleshy Fibres, caused by the Liquor contained in the Nerves, agitated ad Imperium Anima or by the Conftrudipn of the Venous Duds, there be - comes l - m - immund - mM.. i ' i ii ‘ ' r - r - ' - M Y D comes a Repletion of their Cells, whereby the Length of the Fibrillce is contracted. Dr. Chirac, Profeflbr of Medicine at Montpellier, supposes, and thinks he can prove it analytically, That every Muscle being composed of a Vast Multitude of Fibres, like Threads, folded up all together within one Skin or Membrane, and eve - ry Fibre having its proper Vein, Artery, and Nerve, it hath also from Space to Space several Ikrle Cavities or Pores which are of an oblong Form, when the Muscle is slack or flaccid but the Blood circulating through the Muscle, is continually disposing into those Pores a Sulphurous Recrement, abounding with Alkali Salts, which meeting with the Spirits that flow also by the Nerves into those oval Pores, their Nitro - aerial Particles ferment ih a most violent manner with the Saline ones of this Sulphurous Recrement, and thereby distend the Pores so, as to make them change their long oval Figure into a round one j and thus the Muscle ffiuft be contracted.

MUSCLE; a Muscle is only a Bundle f Fibres, which being closely compacted at each end make the two Tendons, each of which is inferred into sore fixt parts of the Body. Every one of these Fibres consists of a prodigious number of lesser Fibril U, which are so many very ( lender Elastick. Canals bound about by small transverse parallel Threads, which divide these hollow Fibrillce into so many Elastick Cyftes or Veficulce, which are or - dicular, being formed of two Concave Segments ofa Sphere. Into every one of these Veficulce, an Artery, Vein and Nerve enter the first to bring and carry back the Blood; the last to carry thither the Licjuidum Nervorum or Nervous Juice, which mingling in the Veficulce, with the Blood, doth ve - ry probably ( it having an Acid tast, and therefore, consisting of Particles which are pointed and so qualified to prick and break;. the Globules of the Blood, ) let out the imprisoned Elastick Air which before was contained in the Globules into those little Veficulce, whereby the Elastick Cells of the Fibres will be blown up, and thereby their Lon - gitudinal Diameters, from Cell to Cell strained and this must contract the length of the whole Fibre, and so move that Organ, to which one of the Tendons is fixt.. This, faith Dr. Cheyne, Phil. Frin. Natural Religion, p. zn. is undoubtedly the true manner of Muscular Motion. . He. thinks also, that the broken Shells of these Globules are carried back by the Veins to the Lungs to be new formed j which is the reason that Muscular Motion is so constantly and uniformly performed, as long as the Blood globules and ani - mal Spirits are in sufficient plenty. , MUSCULUS Tubes nov'us Valfalvce vel PaUtc - Salpingceus, is a Muscle arising Broad and Tendi - nous from rhe Edge of all the lunated part of the Os Palati, several of its Fibres being spread upon the Membrane that covers the Foramen Narium, then growing into a Enall thin Tendon, it is reflect - ed about the Hook - like Process of the inner Ala of the Procejfm Pterigoidceus internus, and is insert - ed carnous into all the membranous, fleilxy and cartilaginous parts of the Tube. Its use is to di - late and keep open this Channel. Myogr. compad rate Specim. p,.

musclevein.c: MUSCLE Vein. This Vein is Two - fold, the Superior and the Inferior. The former arises from the Muscles of the Neck, and the latter from the Upper Muscles of the Breasts; and this sometimes opens into the External Jugular.

musculusstapidis.c: MUSCULUS Stapidis, is a Muscle of the Ear, which lies hid in a Bony Pipe, excavated - in the Os Fetrofum, altnoft at the bottom of the Tympa - num, whence it takes its Origin. Its Belly is big and fleshy, and suddenly forming a very thin Ten - don, which descends to its Infection at the Head of the Stapes: When this a els, it draws the Stapes Upwards, to the Foramen Oval.

musick.c: MUSICK is one of the Seven Sciences, com - monly called Liberal, and comprehended also - a - long the Mathematical as having for its Object Discrete Quantity or Number, but not considering it in the Abftradt, like Arithmetic but with re - lation to Time and Sound, in order to make a de - rightful Harmony. This Science is also Theorical, which exatnineth the Nature and Properties of Concords and Dis - cords, explaining the Proportions between them by Numbers: And Practical, which teaclieth not only Composition, that is to fay, the manner of Composing all forts of Tunes or Airs i but also the Art of singing with the Voice, or playing up - on Musical Instruments. See Vol. i.

musket.c: MUSKET - Jhz efj, in Fortification, are Baskets of about a Foot and half high, and or Inches Diameter at the Bottom, and a full Foot at the top: They are filled with Earth, and are fet on low Parapets or Breast - works, or on such as are beaten down, that the Mufqueteers may fire be - tween them at the Enemy, and yet be tolerably well secured against their Fire,

mute.c: MUTE. ( A Term in Law ) A Prisoner is said to Hand Mute, when he refuses to plead to an In - diclmenr.

mutuleinarchitecture.c: MUTULE, in Architecture, is a kind of Square Modillon, fet under the Cornice of the Doric Order, and so called from the Word Mutilus, Maim ’ d, or Imperfect, because they represent the ends of the Rafters which are crooked or bent; in like manner, as the Beams, or Joints are re - presented by the Triglyphs in the Fri e of trie fame Order.

mydriasis.c: MYDRIASIS, is a too great Dilatation of the Pupil of the Eye, which makes the Sight a Dim, because too much Light is then admitted into the Eye.,,,,. -.

myelosthemarrow.c: MYELOS, the Marrow of the Bones, of bf tllrf Brain, or Spinal Marrow.

myglossum.c: MYGLOSSUM, is a pair of Muscles which arise about the backside of the Grinding Teeth,, and are inserted into the Ligament of the Tongue, -, and are said to turn the Tongue upwards. Blan - chard. These from their Use, I suppose are the fame which our Mr. Cowper calls Styloglofpus, a Muscle,, ' which arising sharp and fleshy from the Process Styloides, descends obliquely forward, and is In - served to the Root of the Tongue immediately below the Implantation of the CeratogloJJ'us: This puts the Tongue inward, and turns it upwards.

mylohoideus.c: MYLOHOIDEUS, is a Muscle which Fallop piui makes double, but Mr. Cowper thinks it a Angle one, not being to be divided without great Violence; It possesses all that Space which is be - tween the Lower Jaw, and the Os Hy aides ari - sing fleshy from both sides of the Mandible Inter - nally, near the Dentes Molares whence marching with a double order of Fleshy Fibres, the out - wardmoft of which pass directly to their Implan - tation in the, Os Ifyoides and the middle run Transversely over the following Muscles, being inseparably joined to each other with a middle Line, as is well exprest by Bidloo, ( Tab. ) Be - tides the Uses commonly ascribed to this Muscle in moving the Os Hyoides, Tongue, and Larynx f upwards, and forwards, and to either side - its last described Transverse Order of Fibres, have still a further use in Compressing the Glandule Sublinguales, which lie immediately under them on each side - whereby they hasten the Egress of the Spittle, from the Inferior Salival Pudts in the Mouth. Hence it is we employ these Muscles ( as in the Action of Deglutition ) when we Wane Saliva to moisten the Mouth: And in that Adliorf also they supply it with frefli Saliva, to join with those Aliments where Mastication is not required which Artifice of Nature deserves onr Admira - tion. Cowper.

mylpha.c: MYLPHA, according to some, the falling off of the Hairs of the Eye - lids; ana with others Medicines against the falling off of the Hair. Blanchard.

myocephalon.c: MYOCEPHALON, is the falling of off a final ! Portion of the Tunica Vvea, just begun, like the Head of a Fly; Whence it has its Name. Blan - chard;

modesplatyfma.c: MODES Platyfma, is a broad Musculous Ex - ' panfion in the Neck, proceeding there from a fort of a fat Membrane. Blanchard.

myologia.c: MYOLOGIA is a Description of the Muscles of an Animal Body.

myopiapurblindness.c: MYOPIA, Purblindness, is a certain Dirnnefs or Confusion of Sight in distant Objects, and yet a Perspicacity in things near at hand: It is occasioned by the Globe of the Eye ’ s being too Convex, so as to unite the Rays before they come to the Petina: Wherefore since the DiftinP: Base falls not on the retina, but perhaps in the Vitrious Humour, the Vision in such an Eye can - not be distinct, unless of Objects very near. But. all such Persons may be helped by Concave Glasses, or SpedtacleS.

myrmecia.c: MYRMECIA, is a fort of Wart; they are harder and lower than those Fleshy Tumours cal - led T hymn, take deeper Root, and occasion great - ter Pain;. broad below - and small at top, and emit less Blood, They are scarce ever bigger than a fort of Pulse called Lupines: They breed in the Palms of the Hand; or the Sole of the ' Foot. Blanchard, N A A NAAAf, in Common Law, signifies a Distress, or the taking another Man ’ s Goods, and is either Lawful, or Unlawful ’, Lawful Naam, is a reasonable Distress, proportionable to the Value of the thing Distrained for.

maggotintimesofpopery.c: MAGGOT, in Times of Popery here, was a Badge worn on the Sleeve of the Upper Garment of such Perfonsas had recanted and abjured what the Powers, that then were, did call Heresy; which was put on after the Poor Wretches had carried a Faggot, by way of Penance, to some ap - pointed Place of Solemnity. And sometimes they interpreted the Leaving off this Badge of the Fag - got to be a Sign of Apoftacy. '

magazineorarsenal.c: MAGAZINE or Arsenal, is the place in For - tified Towns, &c. where all forts of Stores are kept, and where Carpenters, Wheel - wrights, Smiths, s c. are employed in making aH things needful to furnish. out the Train of Artillery.

mag.c: MAG - BOTE, was formerly a Recompence made in Money, or otherwise, for flaying or mur - during one ’ s Kinfinan; for sometimes the Corpo - ral Punishments in such cafes due were tranfmu - ted into Pecuniary Fines; when the Friends or Relations of the Party slain, were so content. Leg. Canuti Regis. T.. c..

magnetism.c: MAGNETISM. See Mr. Durham's Experiments and Reafonitfgs on this Subject in Phil. Trans. N.. where he acquaints us, That he found ( as Grimaldi and De la Hire had in part done before J that a piece of very well touched I - ron Wire would, upon being bent round into a ' Ring, or coil ’ d round upon a Stick, &c. most times quite lose its Verticity, and always have it much diminished thereby. But yet that if the whole length of the Wire were not entirely bent, so that the Ends of it, tho ’ but for the length of one tenth of an Inch, were left strait; then the Vertue would not be destroyed in those parts or ends; tho ’ it would every where else. He found ’ also, on repeated trials, that tho ’ cooling or bending the Wire as abovesaid, would always in the Day - time diminifli and most times destroy the Verticity of a touch ’ d Wire; yet it would not do it in the Eve - nings: And he faith, he knows very well, that the Orb of the A & ivity of Magnets is larger or less a p different times; which is confirmed by what is found in sest to be true of our noble large Load - stone which is kept in the Repository at Grefham College; for that will keep a Key or other piece of Iron suspended to another, sometimes at the distance of or o Foot from it; but at other times, not beyond the distance of four Foot. He found also, that twijiing the Wire would considerably diminifli, and sometimes destroy the Verticity; which in some Trials made on twisted Wire, was so confused and dis ordered, that he found by drawing one of the Poles of a Loadstone along near the sides of the Wire, in some places it would. attract M AJ & tra &, in others resell, and so attract and resell all along the Wire; and he sandy ’ d, in fotae places, that one side of the Wire would be attracted and the other repelled by one and the lame Pole. P After this he try ’ d what / flitting or cleaving the Wire would do; and in particular, whether split Wires would have the fame Properties as Load - stones cut asunder, and he found the Phenomena of this Experiment very odd; for sometimes the Poles of the Wire so split would be quite chang ’ d; so that the South Pole would become the North, in all refpeds: Sometimes one half of the Wire would retain its Magnetilm which it had before its splitting, and the other half would have it quite changed, Gfc. He observed also one thing to be very surprising in these split Wires; which was. That laying one, or the other side of the Half uppermost, would cause a great alteration in its Tendency or Aver - sion to the Poles of the Magnet: But if you lay the contrary side of that half uppermost, the fame end Shall be attraded by one and repelled by the Other Pole. In other Pieces where the Ends are regularly attraded or repelled, only in an inverted order ( as if new touched ) if it lay with the round side uppermost. at that time, and be then turned upfide down, vis - the flat cleft side uppermost; ft is ten to one, he faith that one of the Ends is ei - ther attraded by bots the; Poles, or repelled by both; Or else attraded and repelled by one, and in hclitation by the other. He touched a Wire from end to end with only one Pole of the Magnet; which gave - it so vig - rous a vertue that he is almost of opinion tie the best way of touchings the consequence was, that the end where he began always turned contrary to the Pole that touched it: He then touched the fame Wire ( and others likewise ) with the other Pole of the fame Magnet, from the fame end, and then that end turned the contrary way. For instance, mark one end of the Wire for the North End, and touch that Wire by drawing the North Pole of the Magnet, divers times along the Wire from the North to the South End: This Wire so touched shall have a vigorous Verticity; but the North End shall stand South. But if you touch that or Ano - ther Wire, sor it is all one, the latter touch de - stroking the former ) by drawing the North Pole of the Magnet from the South to the North End of the Wire, then this North End will turn North: And so it will be if you touch with the Southern Pole from the North to the South. He found also, that if he touch ’ d an Iron Wire exadfly in the middle with but one Pole of the Loadstone without drawing it backwards or for - wards, in that place would be the Pole of the Wire and the two Ends would be the contrary Pole of the Wire, and were accordingly repelled or attrifted by the Poles of the Magnet; and, the middle, and about. an. Inch more on each side, Was attraded only by the Pole that touched it.

mile.c: MILE, was anciently a kind of Money, as some think; for Mailes were Half - pence in Henry the Fifth ’ s time; being the half of the Silver Ster - ling or Penny: But more largely it feetiis to have been any proportion of Grain, or any other Bpnt. This latter in the North is called Blackmail. See ' Blackmail in Vob I.

mainbody.c: MAIN BODY, of Troops in an Army, is that which marches between the Advance and the Bear Volt IB Gua ? d and in a Camp, that which lies between the Wings.;;,

maletent.c: MALE TENT, or Maletolte; in the Statute cal - led the Confirmation of the Liberties, Ed.. c. yl is interpreted to be a Toll of s. for every Sack of Wool; and in the Statute de Tallagio non con - cedendo in the Year of the fame King Ed,.. ’ tis appointed, that nothing for hereafter shall be taken of Sacks of Wool, under the pretence of Maletent. It seems to come from Malum Tele - nium.

mal.c: MAL - VOISIN, was formerly the name of a Warlike Engine used in battering of Walls to calf Stones &c. It was so called, because it was an ill or dangerous Neighbour.

manica.c: MANICA, was formerly a square piece of Gold, commonly Valued at Pence; and Mancufa was as much as a Mark, of Silver. See Canute ’ laws. ’ Twas called Mancufa, quaff Manu cus. MANCUSA. See Manca.,,

mancipleacaterer.c: MANCIPLE, a Caterer; there was ancient -, ly an Officer in the Temple called by this Name, now the Steward, And the Name and Office is retained still in our Colleges, in both our Univer - cities.

manse.c: MANSE, is a Parsonage or Vicarage House for the Incumbent to. live in, and was originally, and is now, an essential part of the Endowment of a, Parilb - Church, together with the Glebe and Tithes. : MANUALIA Beneficial were formerly filch daily distribution of portions of Meat and Drink, as were allotted to the petty Canons and other Members of Cathedral Churches for their ordinal - ry subsistence.

manumission.c: MANUMISSION, is the Term for making a Slave or a Bondman free: You have the form of this as it wds used in the Cohquerour s Time, in Lambert ’ s ' A euovoula, Fob. The Terms of the Laxb rake tWo kinds of Manumission one ' ex - pressed and the other imply ed That expressed whs by Deed, or Publick. Declaration: That imply ed was when the Lord made an Obligation for pay - ment of Money to his Villain at a certain day; or seed him when he might enter Without Suit C of or when he granted him an Annuity or Lealed Land to him for Years, or for Life, &c.

manu.c: MANU - OPERA, are stolen Goods taken up - on a Thief apprehended in the Fadfc.
MANU - PASTUS, in the Law Dialed is often used for a Domeftick Servant, one fed as it were by the Hand of his Matter.
MANU - PES, is used in the Charter of Richard the Third for a Foot of full and legal length.
MANU - PRISON, one who was Bail - pledge or Security for another Person.

manus.c: MANUS j was anciently used both for an Oath and him that took it. If a Man swore a - lone in the Court; he was said to do it frofrih manu; but if he brought or more Witnesses to swear for him, he was laid tcrtia manu fur are.

MARCHES, are now the Bounds between England and Wales, or England and Scotland and the Marches of Scotland are divided into Weft and Middle Marches. The word Marches is used also in St at.. H... for the Borders of the King ’ s Dominions in general, as being derived from the Germ. March, which lignifies a Bound or Limit j stand those Noblemen who lived near these Marches, are frequently in our Statutes called Marchers.

maritagium.c: MARITAGIUM habere, signified formerly to have th free disposal of an Heiress in Marriage, which was a favour granted by the King, who was the Guardian of all Wards or Heirs in Mi - novity, to some special Favourite or Friend.

maritagiumliberum.c: MARITAGIUM Liberum, Frank. Marriage j ivas when a Baron, Knight or Free - holder grant - ed such a part of his Estate with a Daughter to her Husband, and the Heirs of his Body, to hold without any Homage or Service to the Donor.

markthesaxons.c: MARK, the Saxons called it Mancus, Mancufa and Me arc; and among them it contained Pence, which of their Money was Shillings. ’ Tis not certain when the Mark, came to be valued as at s. d. But M. Paris in the Life of Gua - rinus. Abbot of St. Albans, tells us, that a Mark A. D. ) was of this precise value. Since the Conquest there never was any Coin of this name struck, as appears; but probably there might be such before in the Saxons time, and with some Mark, or Stamp upon it, as may be concluded from the word Mark. Stovr in his Annals, p., &, faith, a Mark of Gold was eight Ounces, twelve Mark of Gold Troy was /. of Englijh Money; after which rate each Mark weighed. r s. d. Skene de VerLfignif. faith, a Mark lignifies an Ounce weight, whereof the Drachm is the eighth part, as the Ounce is the eighth of the Mark -

marquess.c: MARQUESS before an Earl, and next af - ter a Duke. The Name seems to be derived from the Germ. March, a Bound or Limit; and there - fore was as much as Custos Limitis, or Comes five prafeStus Limitis. Among the old Britains it was the Custom, and after them of the Saxons, to give the Title of Reguli to all Lords that had the custom - dy and charges of their Marches or Bounds as Sel - den shews in his Mare Clausum, Lib.. c.. But in Richard. his time, the Title of Marqueffes in - stead of Lords Marches came to be given to such as were Governours of the Marches.

mars.c: MARS. Mr. Flamflead and CaJJini have by ac - curate Oblervgtion found the Horizontal Parallax of this Planet to be about Seconds, and cer tainly not greater; a large account of the method of observing and finding which, you will find un - der the word Sun in this Vol. MA. RTYRQLGGY, was anciently a Register kept in the Religious Houses, wherein they fet down the Donations of their Benefadors, and the Day of their Deaths, that so on each Anniversary they might commemorate and pray for them: And therefore several Benefadors made this a Conditi - on in their Charters. Rennets Paroch. Antiq.

massesinpainting.c: MASSES, in Painting, are the large parts of a Pidure containing the great Lights and Shadows.

materiasuh.c: MATERIA Suh tills, in the Cartesian Philofo - phy is what is produced by the grinding or rub - bing one against another of the Particles of the second Elements; and so these compose what he calls his first Element. See Cartesian Syfi. of the World in this d VoL

matricula.c: MATRICULA, anciently was the word for a Register. Thus in the Church ' there was the Ma - tricula Cleri corum, which was a Lift or Catalogue of the officiating Clergy; and Matricula Paupe - rum f a Catalogue of the Poor to be received and ‘ II. to this day being Regiftred as a Member in the University of Oxon is called Matriculation.

matrosses.c: MATROSSES, are Soldiers in the Train of Artillery, ' next - below the Gunners: Their Dhty is to assist the Gunners in Traversing, Spunging Firing and Loading of Guns,. ( c. They carry Fire - locks and march along with the Store Wag - gons.

maund.c: MAUND, was anciently a Measure of Capa - city with us, being a kind of great Basket or Hamper containing Bales, or Fates. See the Book of Rates, sol..

may.c: MAY, is the Tin - miners Term for a Weed, as they call it, of. the Marchafite kind, from whence Maxy seems to be a Corruption. When the Load. or Vein of Ore degenerates into this or any thing else that is not Tin, they call it a Weed.

But Custom in Time hath prevailed against this, having altered Mea. fures as well as Weights; no other but Troy Weight being appointed by our Laws to be used, ( See and of Ed;. ) vVe having now different Measures; vig. one for Wine, one for Ale and Beer, and one for Corn. See the Table of them under Measures, Vol. I. Only let me add further from Mr, John Ward's Arithmetick, p.. Mead, Perry, Sider, Vinegar, Oyl, Honey, ( c. are mea - sure d and fold, is supposed to contain Cubicle Inches; and from thence, the Tierce will contain ’ Cub. membrettoinarchitecture.c: MEMBRETTO, in Architecture, is the Italian Term for a Pilafter, that bears up an Arch, These are often fluted, but not with above or Channels. They are frequently used to adorn Door - Cafes, Gallery Fronts, and Chimney Pieces, and to bear up the Cornilhes and Freezes in Wain - scot.

mensals.c: MENSALS J as were united formerly to the Tables of Religious Houses; and therefore are by Canonifts called Merfal Benefices.

merchentlage.c: MERCHENTLAGE was one of those Laws out of which W. the Conqueror framed our Common Laws, with a mixture of the Laws of Normandy and was the Law of the Mercians when they go - verned a third part of this Land for it was di - vided in the Year. See Cambdens Britan - nia, p..

merchetummerchet.c: MERCHETUM, Merchet, in Scorch Marches, was anciently a Commutation of Money or Cat - tle given to the Lord to buy off that old Impious Custom of the Lord ’ s lying the first Night with the Bridal Daughter of a Tenant; and " after it was used for the Fine or Composition which the Tenants paid to have leave to marry their Daugh - ters: Also nO Baron or Military Tenant could marry his some Daughter or Heir, without Licence from the King pro maritanda Filia.

mercurialphofphorm.c: MERCURIAL Phofphorm, is a Light arising from the shaking of Mercury in Vacuo of which fee several Experiments in Philo f Trarf N., See Phosphorus.

mesolabium.c: MESOLABIUM. See Renati Tran. Fluff Me - folabium; cui acceffit pars alter de analyst & Mifcel - lanea. Leodii Ehuronum... to.

messenger.c: MESSENGER of the Exchequer: The four Pur - suivant in that Court are called by this Name, and their Duty and Office is to attend the Lord, Treasurer, and to carry his Letters, Precepts, &c.

messuage.c: MESSUAGE, is a Dwelling - house, with some Land assigned for its use; and by this Name a Garden, Shop, Mill, Chamber or Cellar may pass, faith Plowden, sol.. In Scotland it is what we call the Mannor House, the principal Dwelling - House within any Barony.

metteshepmettefchep.c: METTESHEP, Mettefchep, Mettenfcep, seems to have been anciently a Fine or Penalty paid by the Tenant to his Lord for his negleCt or omiiuon of doing his customary Service. Perhaps it should be written Mittenfcep from the Saxon Mitten, to measure, and cap, Goods or Chattels.

micrography.c: MICROGRAPHY, is the Description of the Parts and Properties of such very small Objects as are only discernible by means of the Microfcoper On this SubjeCt the late Dr. Hook hath written de - feignedly in his Micrography, as hath also Dr. Pow - er and Leuenhoeck, in Vol. in Quarto, Lat. in which, as well as scattered up and down in many other Books written on other Subjects, a very Noble Treasure of useful Difcovefies is to be found, and all made by means of the Microscope.

middlelatitude.c: MIDDLE Latitude, in Navigation, is half the Summ of any two given Latitudes; as suppose the two Latitudes were. '. and., '. the middle Latitude will be.. There is a method of working the several Cafes of Sailing by Middle Latitude, which nearly agrees with Mercator ’ s or Wrights way; and it is per - formed without the Tables of Meridional Parts, either by the Tables of Logarithms or by Gunters Scales. Of this Method you have a short Synopsis in Mr. Jones ’ s Navigation, p.. MID - SHIP - MEN, are Officers aboard a Ship, whose Station when they are on Duty is some on the Quarter - Deck, others on the Poop, ( Sc. Their Business is to mind the Braces, to look out, and tO give about the word of command, from the Captain and other superiour Officers. They do also afllft on all occasions both in failing the Ship and in string and rummaging the Hold.. They are usually Gentlemen who having served their Time as Voluntiers are now upon their pre - ferment.

miliarisglamittg.c: MILIARIS Glamittg ) are those very small and infinitely numerous Glands which secern the Sweat and the Matter that exsuded in insensible perspire - tion. See Skin.

miniumorbedlead.c: MINIUM or Bed Lead. Mr. Bay at the end of his Colled:, of Engl, words gives this account of the making of Minium. First they take Lead and waft it in an Oven or Furnace; by bringing ic to a Substance almost like Litharge, and by stirring about with an Iron Rake or Hoe. Then they take it out and grind it with two pair of Stones which deliver it from one to another; and there is a Mill which moves at once fix pair of these Stones. When ’ tis thus reduced to a Powder, they wafli it, and then put it into an Oven or Re - verberatory Furnace, where by continual stirring with a Rake or Hoe of Iron it comes to its Co - lour in or days. But the Fire must not be violent, for then it will clod and change Colour. The Iron Rake is hung or poised by a Hook, else it would be too heavy to be moved by one Man.

mint.c: MINT,. is the place where the King or Queen ’ s Coin is formed, be it of Gold or Silver: The chief Mint of England is in the lower of London; of which the present Officers are, (. ) The War - den, who - is the chief and is to receive the Bullion, and oversee all the other Officers, ( ij T he Aia - fler Worker, who receives the Bullion from the Warden, causes it to be melted and delivered to the Moniers, and takes it from them again when coined. - (. ) Comptroller; who is to fee that the Money be made to the just assize, and to verfee and controll the Officers, if the Money be not as it ought to be. (. ) The Ajfay Master, who Weighs the Silver and Gold, and fees whether it be Stan - dard. (. ) The Auditor who takes all the Ac - counts. (. ) ‘ The Surveyor of the Melting, who is to see the Silver Call out, and that it be not alter ’ d af - ter it ’ s delivered to the Mel ter; which is after the Ajjay - Masser hath made trial of ir. (. ) The Clerk of the Irons, who is to fee that the Iron be clean and fit to work With. (. ) The Graver, who graveth the Dies and Stamps for the Coinage of the Mo - new. (. ) The Melters, who melt the Bullion be - fore it comes to coining. ( o. ) TheBlanchers, who anneal. Boil and cleanse the Money, The porters, who keep the Gate of the Mint. (. ) The Proves of the Mint, who provides for all the Mo - niers, and overseer them. And lastly, the Moni - es, some of which shear the Money, some forge it, and some stamp or coin it, and some round it and mill it, ( Sc.

mittedabbots.c: MITTED Abbots, were formerly Governours of such Religious Houses, as had obtained from ' Borne the Privilege of wearing the Nitre, Ring, Crosier, and Gloves of a Bishop. It hath been a vulgar Error, that these Mitred Abbots were all the fame with those Conventual Prelates who were summoned to Parliament as Spiritual Lords; but some of those summoned to Parliament were not mitted; and some that were mitted were not sum - moned; the Summons to Parliament not any way depending on their Mitres, but on their receiving their Temporals from the King. Cowel ’ s Inter - prefer.

moat.c: MOAT; the Brink of the Moat next the Ramd part in any Fortification is called the Scarp, and the opposite one the Counterscarp.

model.c: MODEL, is an original Pattern which any Workman proposes to imitate; ’ tis variously made of Wood, Stone, Plaster, ( Sc. and should be ( in Architecture, for instance ) made by a Scale, where an Inch or half an Inch represents a Foot, for the more exact compleating of the design.

molmutanormolmutinlaws.c: MOLMUTAN or Molmutin Laws, were the Laws of Dunwallo Molmutius, sixteenth King of the Britains; they were famous here till the Time of William the Conqueror. Molmutius was the first that published Laws in Britain; and these Laws, with those of Queen Mercia, are published in Latin by Gildas, out of the British Tongue.

monopolizers.c: MONOPOLIZERS, are luch Persons as co m - bine together to engross, and co raise the Price of Goods.

monsoons.c: MONSOONS, are drifting trade Winds In the E. Indian Ocean, which blow periodically, some , for for half a Year one way, others but for Months, and then slusy and blow for or Months dired - ly contrary.

moors.c: MOORS: The Lords Bayliffs in the Isle of Man are called by this Name their Office is to summon the Courts for the several Sheadings.

moralphilosophyormoraldiscipline.c: MORAL Philosophy or Moral Discipline, Is what is usually call ’ d Ethickj in the Schools, be - ing a radical Science which " explains the Nature and Reason of, and withal teaches and Inftruds us how to acquire that Felicity or Happiness which is agreeable to Humane Nature.

moral.c: MORAL AElions or Ads, are such as render the Rational and Free Agent good or evil, and cone - quently rewardable and punishable, because he doth them.

moresk.c: MORESK - Work of Moriskp - tVork, is a kind of Antick - work in Painting or Sculpture, after - the manner of the Moors, consisting of several Gro - tefco's.

morsusdiaboli.c: MORSUS Diaboli, is the Term which feme Anatomists give to the outer Ends ( A e. those next the Ovaria ) of the Tube Fallopian because their Edges there appear jagged and torn.

mortars.c: MORTARS of Mr. Coehorn, are made of Hammer ’ d Iron of. about Inches Diameter at the Bore, ten Inches and a half long, and nine Inches in the Chafe. They are fixed at an Eleva - tion Of. oh a Block of Oak of about Inches long and o - i broad, and about thick. These like Hand - Mortars, throw Hand - Grenadoes. They are used chiefly in the bottom of the Trenches where they are placed about a Yard distance one from another, having each a Soldier to attend it and there is an Officer to every or of them. ’ D They MOT M U L They fire sometimes or of these together, which throw their Shells into the Covertway, cc, and make a very terrible daughter.

mortiseormortaife.c: MORTISE or Mortaife, is the Workmens word in Architecture for the Hole made in one piece of Timber to receive the Tendon of another piece.

mortmainstatute.c: MORTMAIN Statute: There was a Statute made in Ed. I. de Terris in manum mortuam non fonendis to restrain the donation of any Lands or Tenements to Religious or Pious uses, where they lay in a Dead Hand, without Succeilion or due Service to the Lord and the King. After which Statute the Lands so given away were for - feited to the King, if the immediate Lord of the Fee made not his Claim within a Year after such Alienation. When the King by special Licence dispensed with this Statute of Mortmain, there was a previ - ous Inquisition ad quod dampnum, and a return upon Oath that it would be no prejudice to the Dignity and Revenues of the Crown. This Law is now relaxed by St at.. Eli. c.. of giving Lands to Hofpitals; and by of Car. II. c.. a - bout purchasing Lands and Tenements for the Poor within London and TVeftminfier.

mulieraterm.c: MULIER, a Term used in our Common Law some think to be a Corruption either from the Latin Melior or the French Mcilieur, and fignk fies the Lawful Issue preferred before an Elder Brother born out of Matrimony. Others will have it to be derived, quasi ex muliere nattts & non ex concubine; and so they use the word Filius mulse - ratus, in opposition to a Bastard and in thisSenfe the Scotch also use the word, and therefore this last Etymology is most probable.

The Mundicl Ore is easily known by its brown sad - colour ’ d glitter - ing, and by its soon coloring your Fingers. Some fay this nourilhes the Tin, and yet they fay also, where much Mundick. is found there is little or no Tin and his certain,. that if there beany Mun - dicli left in melting the Tin, it makes it thick and ruddy, as they speak; that is, it is not so ductile as otherwise it would be.

What follows is a brief Account of the Elements of Musick. communicated by the In - genious Mr, ffohn Perks. The thing considered in Musick is Flarmonical Sound, or Sound so manageable as to please the Ear and Fanfie of the Hearer. . The Sense of Sound is caused in us by the trembling motion of the Air, excited by the per cushion of some solid Body, as a Bell, String, Pipe, yc. This Trembling of the Air is Quick or Slow, ’ according to the I m predion given by the Voice or Instrument. The quicker the Trembling is, the more acute and sharp is the Sound; and the flower, the more grave and flat. The fame degree of Quickness of the Trem - being or. Pulses of the Air being continued, the fame Sound or Note is continued also, Hence a sounding String keeping the fame Note to the last, shews, that its Vibrations are in equal Time from the greatest to the least Ranges of its motion. M U S The shorter a Musical String is, creteris paribus, the quicker are its Vibrations, and the more acute its Note: And, contrary wife, the longer a String is, the more flow are its Vibrations; and the more give its Note. Hence the Proportions of the degrees of Acute - ness and Gravity of Notes are computed from the Divisions of a Monochord, or strained Musical String. The Proportion of Quickness in the Vibrations of two Strings, and also of the Pulses of the Air excited thereby, is Reciprocal or Counter to the Lengths of the Strings so twice the Length gives ( cateris paribus ) half the Quickness of Pulses ( or half the number of Pulses in the fame time;, ) If the Lengths are as to, the Velocity of Pulses is as to, &c, Hence the Relation or Proportion of Musical Notes is determined as follows. When two Notes in any of the precedent Pro - portions one to another, are founded together their Sounds are agreeable and pleasing to the Ear and are therefore called Concords. Of these the Eighth and Fifth are called PerfeB Concords '; Thirds and Sixths are called ImperfeB Concords The Fourth anciently accounted a Concord ) Is by Modern Muficians accounted a Discord to the Bass in Consort - Musick, as wanting a Fifth under to compleat the Harmony. The above - mentioned are all the Simple Con - cords that the Ear allows of. If the Proportion between any two Notes be compounded of the Pro - portion of an OBave with that of any other Con - cord, it retains the Name and Nature of the added Concord. So a Tenth, that is, an Eight and Third, ' is accounted but a Third; and so of the reft. All other Proportions between Notes ( bund - ing together produce Discords, or Sounds harfli ' and unpleasing to the Ear, the Coincidences of the Pulles being too remote one from the other. By this it appears, that Commenfur ability in the Quickness of the Vibrations is necessary to Concor - dance and the smaller the Numbers are that ex - press the Proportion of the Pulses in the fame Time, ' or the nearer their Coincidences, the more perfeEB is the Harmony. And consequently if their Pulles be of Incommensurable Velocities, the Discord will be in th e higheji degree harfti and displeasing. From this Account of Concords and Dilcords may a Reason be given of several Phenomena of Sounds, as particularly why two Strings of a Bass Viol that are ZJnifons or OBaves one to the other, if one be struck, the other will tremble so as to be sensibly perceived if a small bit of Paper be laid, on it. For the String that is struck putting the Air into a certain degree of trembling, which be - ing the fame, or next degree of Proportional Quickness to that of the unstruck String, sets it a trembling also. This Experiment ( and others of like nature ( Dr. Holder very well illustrate by the Instance of a Pendulum, which if you blow in - to motion, land continue to blow uniformly as ic begins to go from you, it may be continued in motion as long as you please but if you blow ir - regularly ( sometimes as it goes and sometimes as it comes ! its motion will be cheek ’ d and at lalt cease. The reason of which seem to be, that the Times of the Vibra - tions of the loose Quarry were equal ( or in near Concordance ) to those of the String.
